entries.title: Abba
entries.subtitle: The Son's own word for the Father
entries.summary: Jesus addresses God as *Abba*, the Aramaic family word for father. The early church kept the Aramaic word untranslated because it carried the heart of what Jesus shared with them: his own standing with the Father.

data.phrase: Abba, Father
data.greek: αββα ὁ πατήρ (abba ho patēr)

entries.title: The Kingdom of God
entries.subtitle: Basileia: God's reign arriving in Jesus
entries.summary: The central theme of Jesus' preaching. *Basileia* means kingship or reign, God acting as king, more than a place. Jesus announces that it has come near in his own person and work, and his parables describe it growing until it fills the earth.

data.phrase: The kingdom of God / the kingdom of heaven
data.greek: ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ / τῶν οὐρανῶν (hē basileia tou theou / tōn ouranōn)

entries.title: Repent
entries.subtitle: Metanoia: turning around and coming home
entries.summary: Jesus' first recorded command. The Greek *metanoeō* is literally a change of mind, but in the mouth of a Jewish prophet it carries the Hebrew *shuv*: turn back, return home to God.

data.phrase: Repent, and believe the gospel
data.greek: μετανοεῖτε καὶ πιστεύετε ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ (metanoeite kai pisteuete en tō euangeliō)

entries.title: Eternal Life
entries.subtitle: Zōē aiōnios: the life of the age to come, known now
entries.summary: *Zōē aiōnios* means more than endless existence. In Jewish usage it is "the life of the age to come". John defines it relationally: "this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ" (John 17:3).

data.phrase: Eternal life / the life of the age
data.greek: ζωὴ αἰώνιος (zōē aiōnios)

entries.title: Gehenna
entries.subtitle: The Valley of Hinnom and Jesus' warnings
entries.summary: Jesus' word usually translated "hell" is *Gehenna*, the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a place associated with child sacrifice and with the prophets' warning of slaughter. Its meaning is contested: final judgement, a fiery image of ruin, or (on a partial-preterist reading) the catastrophe of AD 70.

data.phrase: Gehenna of fire
data.greek: γέεννα τοῦ πυρός (geenna tou pyros)

entries.title: The Son of Man
entries.subtitle: Jesus' favourite title for himself
entries.summary: Jesus' most frequent self-description. In Aramaic *bar enash* can simply mean "a human being", but Jesus' use draws on Daniel 7, where "one like a son of man" comes to the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion.

data.phrase: The Son of Man
data.greek: ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου (ho huios tou anthrōpou)

entries.title: Take Up Your Cross
entries.subtitle: The way of the crucified king
entries.summary: Jesus' call to deny oneself, take up one's cross and follow him. Before Easter, "cross" meant Roman execution of rebels and slaves; Jesus turns it into the shape of discipleship and of God's own self-giving love.

data.phrase: Take up his cross, and follow me
data.greek: ἀράτω τὸν σταυρὸν αὐτοῦ καὶ ἀκολουθείτω μοι (aratō ton stauron autou kai akoloutheitō moi)

entries.title: Born From Above
entries.subtitle: Anōthen: the birth Nicodemus misheard
entries.summary: Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one can see the kingdom of God unless born *anōthen*, a word that means both "again" and "from above". John uses the double meaning on purpose: the new birth comes from the Father, by the Spirit.

data.phrase: Except a man be born from above (again)
data.greek: ἐὰν μή τις γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν (ean mē tis gennēthē anōthen)

entries.title: I Am
entries.subtitle: Egō eimi: the divine name on Jesus' lips
entries.summary: John's Gospel gathers seven "I am" sayings with images (bread, light, door, shepherd, resurrection, way, vine) and several absolute "I am" sayings with no image at all, which echo God's self-naming in Exodus 3 and Isaiah 40-55.

data.phrase: I am
data.greek: ἐγώ εἰμι (egō eimi)

entries.title: Amen, Amen
entries.subtitle: Truly, truly I say to you
entries.summary: Jesus begins sayings with *Amen* ("truly"), doubled in John. Elsewhere "amen" ends a prayer as the listener's agreement. Jesus puts it first, vouching for his own words with an authority that surprised his hearers.

data.phrase: Verily, verily, I say unto you
data.greek: ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν (amēn amēn legō hymin)

entries.title: Blessed
entries.subtitle: Makarios: the beatitudes' announcement of God's favour
entries.summary: Jesus opens the Sermon on the Mount with "Blessed are...". *Makarios* translates the Hebrew *ʾashrê*, "how fortunate", and in Jesus' mouth it announces that God's kingdom has come to the poor, the mourners and the meek.

data.phrase: Blessed are the poor in spirit
data.greek: μακάριοι οἱ πτωχοὶ τῷ πνεύματι (makarioi hoi ptōchoi tō pneumati)

entries.title: The Father Who Sent Me
entries.subtitle: The Son as the Father's sent one
entries.summary: A refrain of John's Gospel. Jesus constantly describes himself as sent by the Father, doing the Father's works and speaking his words, so that to see and receive the Son is to see and receive the Father.

data.phrase: The Father which hath sent me
data.greek: ὁ πέμψας με πατήρ (ho pempsas me patēr)

entries.title: It Is Finished
entries.subtitle: Tetelestai: the completed work
entries.summary: Jesus' last word in John: *tetelestai*, "it has been completed". It gathers up John's theme of the Son completing the Father's work, and echoes God completing creation on the sixth day.

data.phrase: It is finished
data.greek: τετέλεσται (tetelestai)

entries.title: This Generation
entries.subtitle: Genea: Jesus' time frame for judgement
entries.summary: Jesus says "this generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled" (Matt 24:34). Everywhere else in the Gospels "this generation" means Jesus' contemporaries. Partial preterists read the Olivet prophecy as fulfilled in the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70; others read it differently.

data.phrase: This generation shall not pass
data.greek: οὐ μὴ παρέλθῃ ἡ γενεὰ αὕτη (ou mē parelthē hē genea hautē)

entries.title: The End of the Age
entries.subtitle: Synteleia tou aiōnos: which age ends?
entries.summary: Matthew alone uses "the end of the age" (*synteleia tou aiōnos*): in the parable explanations, in the disciples' Olivet question, and in Jesus' last promise. Partial preterists read it, at least in Matthew 24:3, as the close of the old covenant age in AD 70; most traditions read it as the end of history.

data.phrase: The end of the age (KJV: the end of the world)
data.greek: ἡ συντέλεια τοῦ αἰῶνος (hē synteleia tou aiōnos)

entries.title: My Peace
entries.subtitle: Shalom given by the Son
entries.summary: On the night before his death Jesus gives his disciples "my peace", and after the resurrection his first word to them is "Peace be unto you". Behind the Greek *eirēnē* stands the Hebrew *shalom*: wholeness, right relationship, well-being.

data.phrase: Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you
data.greek: εἰρήνην ἀφίημι ὑμῖν, εἰρήνην τὴν ἐμὴν δίδωμι ὑμῖν (eirēnēn aphiēmi hymin, eirēnēn tēn emēn didōmi hymin)

entries.title: Abide in Me
entries.subtitle: Menō: the vine and the branches
entries.summary: In the vine discourse Jesus uses *menō* (remain, dwell, abide) again and again: "Abide in me, and I in you". It is the Gospel's clearest picture of union with Christ: a shared life, like sap in a vine.

data.phrase: Abide in me, and I in you
data.greek: μείνατε ἐν ἐμοί, κἀγὼ ἐν ὑμῖν (meinate en emoi, kagō en hymin)

entries.title: The Light of the World
entries.subtitle: Light at the Feast of Tabernacles
entries.summary: Jesus says "I am the light of the world" (John 8:12), most likely during the Feast of Tabernacles, when great lamps lit the Temple courts. He also tells his disciples, "Ye are the light of the world" (Matt 5:14).

data.phrase: I am the light of the world
data.greek: ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ φῶς τοῦ κόσμου (egō eimi to phōs tou kosmou)

entries.title: Living Water
entries.subtitle: Hydōr zōn: the Spirit poured out
entries.summary: Jesus offers a Samaritan woman "living water" and cries out at Tabernacles, "If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink". John explains that he meant the Spirit.

data.phrase: Living water
data.greek: ὕδωρ ζῶν (hydōr zōn)

entries.title: The Bread of Life
entries.subtitle: Manna, Passover and the Son's flesh
entries.summary: After feeding five thousand near Passover, Jesus says "I am the bread of life" and claims to be the true manna from heaven, given for the life of the world.

data.phrase: I am the bread of life
data.greek: ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος τῆς ζωῆς (egō eimi ho artos tēs zōēs)

entries.title: The Good Shepherd
entries.subtitle: Ezekiel 34 fulfilled
entries.summary: Jesus calls himself "the good shepherd" who lays down his life for the sheep. The background is Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel's selfish shepherds and promises to shepherd his flock himself.

data.phrase: I am the good shepherd
data.greek: ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός (egō eimi ho poimēn ho kalos)

entries.title: Follow Me
entries.subtitle: Akoloutheō: the call of the rabbi-king
entries.summary: Jesus' call to fishermen, a tax collector and others: "Follow me". Unlike other teachers, Jesus chose his disciples, and following meant sharing his life and road, not only his ideas.

data.phrase: Follow me
data.greek: ἀκολούθει μοι / δεῦτε ὀπίσω μου (akolouthei moi / deute opisō mou)

entries.title: Your Faith Has Made You Whole
entries.subtitle: Sōzō: healed, saved, restored
entries.summary: Jesus says "thy faith hath saved thee" (or "made thee whole") to the woman with the flow of blood, blind Bartimaeus, the sinful woman, and the Samaritan leper. *Sōzō* covers healing, rescue and restoration at once.

data.phrase: Thy faith hath made thee whole / hath saved thee
data.greek: ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε (hē pistis sou sesōken se)

entries.title: Forgive
entries.subtitle: Aphiēmi: release from debt and bondage
entries.summary: The Greek word Jesus uses for forgiving, *aphiēmi*, means to release, let go, send away. It is the language of Jubilee: debts cancelled, captives set free.

data.phrase: Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors
data.greek: ἄφες ἡμῖν τὰ ὀφειλήματα ἡμῶν (aphes hēmin ta opheilēmata hēmōn)

entries.title: The Least of These
entries.subtitle: Christ present in the needy
entries.summary: In the judgement of the nations Jesus says that what was done to "one of the least of these my brethren" was done to him. Who "the least" are is debated: needy people in general, or Jesus' messengers.

data.phrase: Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren
data.greek: ἐφ᾽ ὅσον ἐποιήσατε ἑνὶ τούτων τῶν ἀδελφῶν μου τῶν ἐλαχίστων (eph' hoson epoiēsate heni toutōn tōn adelphōn mou tōn elachistōn)

entries.title: The Narrow Gate
entries.subtitle: Two ways, one road to life
entries.summary: Near the end of the Sermon on the Mount Jesus contrasts the wide gate and broad way that lead to destruction with the narrow gate and hard way that lead to life. It draws on the old Jewish teaching of the "two ways".

data.phrase: Enter ye in at the strait gate
data.greek: εἰσέλθατε διὰ τῆς στενῆς πύλης (eiselthate dia tēs stenēs pylēs)

entries.title: Children of Your Father
entries.subtitle: Love your enemies, and become like your Father
entries.summary: "Love your enemies... that ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven" (Matt 5:44-45). In Jewish idiom, to be "son of" someone is to share his character. The Father's children look like him.

data.phrase: That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven
data.greek: ὅπως γένησθε υἱοὶ τοῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν τοῦ ἐν οὐρανοῖς (hopōs genēsthe huioi tou patros hymōn tou en ouranois)

entries.title: Talitha Koum
entries.subtitle: Little girl, arise
entries.summary: Jesus' Aramaic words to the dead daughter of Jairus, preserved by Mark: "Talitha cumi", "Little girl, I say to you, arise". He takes her by the hand, and she gets up and walks.

data.phrase: Talitha cumi
data.greek: ταλιθα κουμ / κουμι (talitha koum / koumi)

entries.title: Eloi, Eloi, Lema Sabachthani
entries.subtitle: The cry from the cross and Psalm 22
entries.summary: Jesus' cry from the cross in Aramaic: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" It is the first line of Psalm 22, a lament that ends in praise and the conversion of the nations. Its meaning for the relationship of Father and Son is contested.

data.phrase: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
data.greek: ελωι ελωι λεμα σαβαχθανι (elōi elōi lema sabachthani)
data.aramaic: אֱלָהִי אֱלָהִי לְמָא שְׁבַקְתַּנִי (ʾĕlāhî ʾĕlāhî lĕmāʾ šĕbaqtanî)
data.hebrew: אֵלִי אֵלִי לָמָה עֲזַבְתָּנִי (ʾēlî ʾēlî lāmâ ʿăzavtānî)

entries.title: Lost
entries.subtitle: Apollymi: the Father seeks what is his
entries.summary: "The Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost" (Luke 19:10). *Apollymi* means lost, perishing, ruined. In Luke 15, lost things are valuable to their owner, and the owner goes looking.

data.phrase: That which was lost
data.greek: τὸ ἀπολωλός (to apolōlos)

entries.title: Neighbour
entries.subtitle: Plēsion: who is near me?
entries.summary: A lawyer asks "who is my neighbour?" to define the limits of Leviticus 19:18. Jesus answers with the good Samaritan and turns the question round: "which... was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves?"

data.phrase: Who is my neighbour?
data.greek: καὶ τίς ἐστίν μου πλησίον; (kai tis estin mou plēsion?)

entries.title: Hypocrite
entries.subtitle: Hypokritēs: the actor behind the mask
entries.summary: Jesus' word for religious people performing for an audience. *Hypokritēs* was the Greek word for a stage actor, someone who plays a part behind a mask.

data.phrase: Hypocrites
data.greek: ὑποκριταί (hypokritai)

entries.title: The Sower
entries.subtitle: Four soils and an outrageous harvest
entries.summary: A farmer sows seed that falls on the path, on rocky ground, among thorns and on good soil. The good soil yields thirty, sixty and a hundredfold. Jesus explains it as the word of the kingdom and the different ways it is received.

data.setting: Told from a boat to crowds on the shore of the Sea of Galilee.

entries.title: The Seed Growing Secretly
entries.subtitle: The earth bears fruit by itself
entries.summary: A man scatters seed, sleeps and rises, and the seed sprouts and grows, "he knoweth not how". The earth produces the blade, the ear, then the full grain, and at harvest he puts in the sickle. Found only in Mark.

data.setting: Part of Mark's lakeside collection of seed parables.

entries.title: The Mustard Seed
entries.subtitle: From the smallest seed to a tree for the nations
entries.summary: The kingdom is like a mustard seed, the smallest of seeds, that grows into the greatest of garden plants, so that birds nest in its branches.

data.setting: In Mark and Matthew, part of the lakeside teaching; in Luke, after a sabbath healing in a synagogue.

entries.title: The Leaven
entries.subtitle: A woman hides yeast in a huge batch of flour
entries.summary: The kingdom is like leaven that a woman hid in three measures of meal until the whole was leavened. One of Jesus' shortest parables, with a woman as the figure for God's action.

data.setting: Paired with the mustard seed.

entries.title: The Hidden Treasure
entries.subtitle: Joy that sells everything
entries.summary: A man finds treasure hidden in a field, hides it again, and "for joy thereof" sells all he has to buy the field.

data.setting: Told privately to the disciples in the house (Matt 13:36).

entries.title: The Pearl of Great Price
entries.subtitle: The merchant who found one pearl
entries.summary: A merchant seeking fine pearls finds one of great value and sells all he has to buy it.

data.setting: Told privately to the disciples, paired with the hidden treasure.

entries.title: The Dragnet
entries.subtitle: A net that gathers every kind
entries.summary: The kingdom is like a net cast into the sea that gathers fish of every kind. When full, it is drawn ashore and the good are kept, the bad thrown away. "So shall it be at the end of the age."

data.setting: Told privately to disciples, several of whom were fishermen.

entries.title: The Wheat and the Weeds
entries.subtitle: Let both grow together until the harvest
entries.summary: An enemy sows darnel among a farmer's wheat. The servants want to pull it up, but the master says to let both grow until harvest, so the wheat is not uprooted.

data.setting: Told to the crowds by the lake; explained to the disciples in the house.

entries.title: The Lost Sheep
entries.subtitle: The shepherd who goes after the one
entries.summary: A man with a hundred sheep loses one, leaves the ninety-nine and searches until he finds it, carries it home on his shoulders and calls his friends to rejoice.

data.setting: Luke: answering Pharisees and scribes who grumbled that Jesus received sinners and ate with them. Matthew: teaching disciples about "little ones" in the community.

entries.title: The Lost Coin
entries.subtitle: A woman sweeps the house
entries.summary: A woman with ten silver coins loses one, lights a lamp, sweeps the house and searches carefully until she finds it, then calls her friends and neighbours to rejoice.

data.setting: The second panel of Luke 15, told to grumbling Pharisees and scribes.

entries.title: The Lost Son and the Elder Brother
entries.subtitle: The father who runs, and the son who will not come in
entries.summary: A younger son demands his inheritance, wastes it in a far country and returns hoping to be a hired servant. His father runs to meet him and restores him with a feast. The elder son refuses to join in, and the father goes out to plead with him too. The story ends open.

data.setting: The third and climactic panel of Luke 15, told to Pharisees and scribes who grumbled that Jesus ate with sinners.

entries.title: The Good Samaritan
entries.subtitle: Who proved to be a neighbour?
entries.summary: A man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho is robbed and left half dead. A priest and a Levite pass by. A Samaritan stops, treats his wounds, carries him to an inn and pays for his care.

data.setting: Answer to a lawyer (expert in the law) testing Jesus with the question of eternal life and "who is my neighbour?"

entries.title: The Rich Fool
entries.subtitle: A man who talked only to himself
entries.summary: A rich man's land yields so much that he plans bigger barns and tells his soul to eat, drink and be merry. God says, "Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee".

data.setting: Response to a man who asked Jesus to make his brother divide the inheritance.

entries.title: The Great Banquet
entries.subtitle: The invited refuse; the outcasts come in
entries.summary: A man prepares a great supper and invites many, but when the meal is ready the guests make excuses. He sends his servant to bring in the poor, crippled, blind and lame, and then those on the roads and hedges, so that his house may be filled.

data.setting: At a meal in the house of a leading Pharisee on the sabbath, after a guest says "Blessed is he that shall eat bread in the kingdom of God".

entries.title: The Shrewd Manager
entries.subtitle: A steward gambles on his master's mercy
entries.summary: A manager accused of wasting his master's goods is dismissed. Before he leaves, he calls in his master's debtors and reduces their bills. The master praises him for acting shrewdly.

data.setting: Told to the disciples, with Pharisees "who were covetous" listening (Luke 16:14).

entries.title: The Rich Man and Lazarus
entries.subtitle: A great gulf, and Moses and the prophets
entries.summary: A rich man feasts daily while a poor man named Lazarus lies at his gate. Both die: Lazarus is carried to Abraham's side; the rich man is in torment in Hades. Abraham says that if the brothers will not hear Moses and the prophets, they will not be persuaded though one rose from the dead.

data.setting: Told to Pharisees "who were covetous" and derided Jesus (Luke 16:14).

entries.title: The Persistent Widow
entries.subtitle: An unjust judge and a widow who will not stop
entries.summary: A judge who fears neither God nor man refuses a widow's plea for justice, but gives in because she keeps coming. Jesus contrasts him with God, who will quickly vindicate his elect who cry to him.

data.setting: Told to the disciples after teaching about the coming of the Son of Man (Luke 17:20-37).

entries.title: The Pharisee and the Tax Collector
entries.subtitle: Two men went up to the Temple to pray
entries.summary: A Pharisee thanks God that he is not like other men, while a tax collector stands far off, beats his breast and says "God be merciful to me a sinner". The tax collector goes home justified.

data.setting: Told to "certain which trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others" (Luke 18:9).

entries.title: The Labourers in the Vineyard
entries.subtitle: The last will be first
entries.summary: A landowner hires workers at dawn, nine, noon, three and five o'clock. At evening he pays everyone a full day's wage, starting with the last. The first grumble; he asks, "is thine eye evil, because I am good?"

data.setting: Told to the disciples after Peter's question "what shall we have therefore?" (Matt 19:27).

entries.title: The Two Sons
entries.subtitle: Who did the father's will?
entries.summary: A father asks two sons to work in the vineyard. The first says "I will not" but later goes; the second says "I go, sir" but does not. The tax collectors and prostitutes are going into the kingdom ahead of the chief priests and elders.

data.setting: In the Temple during Holy Week, to the chief priests and elders who had challenged Jesus' authority.

entries.title: The Wicked Tenants
entries.subtitle: The vineyard, the servants and the beloved son
entries.summary: A man plants a vineyard and leases it to tenants. They beat and kill the servants he sends to collect fruit, and finally kill his beloved son. The owner will destroy them and give the vineyard to others. The rejected stone becomes the cornerstone.

data.setting: In the Temple during Holy Week, to chief priests, scribes and elders, who "perceived that he had spoken the parable against them".

entries.title: The Wedding Feast
entries.subtitle: The king's son's wedding and the guest without a garment
entries.summary: A king prepares a wedding for his son. The invited guests refuse, mistreat and kill his servants. The king destroys their city and fills the hall with people from the roads, good and bad. One guest without a wedding garment is cast out.

data.setting: The third parable of judgement in the Temple during Holy Week.

entries.title: The Ten Virgins
entries.subtitle: Lamps, oil and a delayed bridegroom
entries.summary: Ten bridesmaids wait with lamps for a bridegroom. Five bring extra oil; five do not. When he arrives at midnight, the foolish are out buying oil and find the door shut.

data.setting: Part of the Olivet discourse, spoken to disciples on the Mount of Olives during Holy Week.

entries.title: The Talents
entries.subtitle: Faithful servants and the one who was afraid
entries.summary: A man going on a journey entrusts five, two and one talents to three servants. Two double the money; the third buries his. On his return the master rewards the faithful and condemns the third, who says, "I was afraid".

data.setting: Part of the Olivet discourse, after the ten virgins.

entries.title: The Pounds
entries.subtitle: A nobleman who went to receive a kingdom
entries.summary: A nobleman goes to a far country to receive a kingdom; his citizens send a delegation saying they will not have him reign. He gives ten servants a mina each. On his return he rewards the faithful, judges the fearful servant and the rebellious citizens.

data.setting: On the road near Jericho, as Jesus approached Jerusalem, "because they thought that the kingdom of God should immediately appear" (Luke 19:11).

entries.title: The Sheep and the Goats
entries.subtitle: The judgement of the nations
entries.summary: When the Son of Man comes in glory, all nations are gathered before him and separated as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. Those who fed, welcomed, clothed and visited "the least of these my brethren" did it to him.

data.setting: The conclusion of the Olivet discourse, spoken to disciples on the Mount of Olives.

entries.title: The Unforgiving Servant
entries.subtitle: Ten thousand talents and a hundred denarii
entries.summary: A king forgives a servant an unpayable debt of ten thousand talents. The servant then seizes a fellow servant who owes him a hundred denarii and throws him in prison. The king revokes the forgiveness.

data.setting: Told in answer to Peter's question, "how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?"

entries.title: The Two Debtors
entries.subtitle: Simon the Pharisee and the woman who loved much
entries.summary: At a meal in Simon the Pharisee's house a sinful woman weeps on Jesus' feet, wipes them with her hair, kisses and anoints them. Jesus tells of a creditor who forgave two debtors, one five hundred denarii and one fifty, and asks which will love him more.

data.setting: A banquet in the house of Simon, a Pharisee, in Galilee.

entries.title: The Friend at Midnight
entries.subtitle: Hospitality and the sleeping neighbour
entries.summary: A man receives an unexpected guest at midnight, has no bread, and goes to wake a neighbour who is in bed with his children. Because of his *anaideia*, the neighbour gets up and gives him what he needs.

data.setting: Told to the disciples straight after Jesus teaches them the Lord's Prayer (Luke 11:1-4).

entries.title: The Barren Fig Tree
entries.subtitle: One more year
entries.summary: A man has a fig tree in his vineyard that has borne no fruit for three years. He orders it cut down, but the vinedresser asks for one more year to dig around it and fertilise it.

data.setting: Told after news of Galileans killed by Pilate and the tower of Siloam falling, with Jesus' warning "except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish".

entries.title: New Wine and Old Wineskins
entries.subtitle: Patches, wineskins and the bridegroom
entries.summary: Asked why his disciples do not fast, Jesus says wedding guests cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them, no one sews unshrunk cloth on an old garment, and no one puts new wine into old wineskins.

data.setting: A dispute over fasting with disciples of John and of the Pharisees, following Jesus' meal with tax collectors at Levi's house.

entries.title: The Lamp Under a Bushel
entries.subtitle: Light is meant to be seen
entries.summary: No one lights a lamp to hide it under a measuring basket or a bed; it is set on a lampstand to give light. What is hidden will be revealed.

data.setting: Matthew: the Sermon on the Mount. Mark and Luke: after the parable of the sower.

entries.title: The Wise and Foolish Builders
entries.subtitle: Building on rock or on sand
entries.summary: Whoever hears Jesus' words and does them is like a man who built his house on rock; the storm came and it stood. Whoever hears and does not is like one who built on sand, and great was its fall.

data.setting: The ending of the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew) and the Sermon on the Plain (Luke).

entries.title: The Budding Fig Tree
entries.subtitle: Learn the lesson of the fig tree
entries.summary: When the fig tree's branch becomes tender and puts out leaves, you know summer is near. So when you see these things, know that it is near. "This generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled."

data.setting: The Olivet discourse, on the Mount of Olives, looking across at the Temple.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/abba
blocks.body:
*Abba* is Aramaic, the everyday language of Galilee. It is the emphatic form of *ʾab* ("father"), so it means "the father" or "my father", and it was the ordinary word a child or an adult child used at home.

The Hebrew Scriptures call God Father rarely and mostly corporately: Israel is God's firstborn son (Exod 4:22; Hos 11:1), and God is "our Father" (Isa 63:16; 64:8). Second Temple prayers sometimes address God as "our Father, our King". What is unusual in the Gospels is how constantly Jesus speaks of "my Father" and "your Father", and that he prays to God with the household word.

Mark keeps the Aramaic and then translates it: *abba ho patēr* (Mark 14:36). Paul does the same in two Greek letters (Rom 8:15; Gal 4:6), which shows that Greek-speaking churches prayed with Jesus' own word.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/abba
blocks.body:
To Jesus' disciples, *abba* was the word of the family table, not of the Temple liturgy. Hearing a teacher pray this way in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36), and then being taught to say "Father" themselves (Luke 11:2), placed them inside the relationship Jesus had with God.

Paul assumes his Gentile readers know the Aramaic cry. It is the Spirit who cries *Abba* in us (Gal 4:6), the "Spirit of adoption" (Rom 8:15). The first Christians heard the word as a sign that they had been brought into the Son's own place.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/abba
blocks.body:
A popular claim says *abba* meant "Daddy", a toddler's word. That overstates the evidence. Adult children also called their fathers *abba*, and the Gospels translate it with the ordinary *ho patēr*, not a diminutive.

The opposite mistake is to say the word is unremarkable. The intimacy lies less in baby-talk than in the settled, family trust of a son who knows he is loved and obeys from inside that love, even in Gethsemane. Both sides agree that Jesus' constant "my Father" stands out against the prayers of his time.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/abba
blocks.body:
*Abba* is the centre of the gospel in one word. Jesus did not come to tell us that God has a father-like side; he came as the eternal Son who has always known the Father, and he shares that knowing with us (Matt 11:27; John 17:26).

Adoption (*huiothesia*) is not a legal fiction filed in heaven. It is the Spirit placing the Son's own cry in our mouths (Gal 4:6). When we pray "Abba", we are praying from inside the Trinity's shared life, with Jesus, not at a distance from God.

Because Jesus is the clearest picture of the Father (John 14:9), the God Jesus calls *Abba* is exactly as trustworthy and kind as Jesus is.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/kingdom-of-god
blocks.body:
*Basileia* translates Hebrew *malkût* and Aramaic *malkû*: kingship, rule, reign. The Psalms sing "The LORD reigns" (Ps 93:1; 97:1), and Daniel promises a kingdom that the God of heaven will set up, which "shall never be destroyed" and will fill the whole earth (Dan 2:35, 44; 7:13-14, 27).

Under Roman rule many Jews longed for God to act as king: to end exile, judge oppressors and restore Israel. Movements ranged from quiet waiting to armed revolt.

Matthew usually says "kingdom of heaven". This follows the Jewish habit of reverently avoiding God's name ("heaven" for "God"). It means the same as Mark and Luke's "kingdom of God", not a kingdom located in the sky.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/kingdom-of-god
blocks.body:
When Jesus said "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand" (Mark 1:15), Galilean hearers would hear: the long-awaited moment in Daniel's timetable has arrived, and God is taking his throne.

They would not have heard "here is how to go to heaven when you die". They would have asked: who is the king, what happens to Rome, what happens to the Temple? Jesus' answers surprised them: the kingdom arrives through healing, forgiveness, table fellowship with sinners and, finally, a cross (Matt 12:28; Luke 7:22).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/kingdom-of-god
blocks.body:
Two common misreadings shrink the kingdom. One treats it as heaven after death, a place souls go. The other postpones it entirely to a future millennium, so that it has no real presence now.

Jesus says it has "come upon you" already (Matt 12:28) and is "in your midst" (Luke 17:21). He also teaches us to pray for it to come "on earth, as it is in heaven" (Matt 6:10). The kingdom is God's reign arriving now, through the Son, in this world, and growing.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/kingdom-of-god
blocks.body: N. T. Wright reads Jesus' kingdom announcement within Israel's story: Israel was still in a kind of exile, and Jesus claimed that the return from exile and the return of Israel's God to Zion were happening in and through his own ministry. The kingdom, on this reading, is God's rescue of the world through Israel's Messiah, not an escape from the world.

citations.ref: Jesus and the Victory of God (on the kingdom announcement)

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/kingdom-of-god
blocks.body: Postmillennial writers such as Loraine Boettner read the kingdom parables of growth (mustard seed, leaven) as describing a reign that steadily spreads through the preaching of the gospel until the world is largely Christianised before Christ's return.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/kingdom-of-god
blocks.body:
The kingdom is the Father's family rule breaking into the world through his Son. It looks like Jesus: the sick healed, the excluded welcomed to the table, enemies forgiven, death defeated.

It began small (a seed, a little leaven) and it is growing. That is why the lens of this app is hopeful about history: the risen Christ reigns now (Matt 28:18), and "of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end" (Isa 9:7). To enter the kingdom is to come home to the Father under the rule of his Son.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/repent
blocks.body:
*Metanoeō* is formed from *meta* (after, change) and *noeō* (to think, perceive). In ordinary Greek it can mean to change one's mind or regret.

Jesus spoke Aramaic, and his call would have sounded like the prophets' Hebrew *shuv*, "turn back, return". Hosea pleads "O Israel, return unto the LORD thy God" (Hos 14:1); Jeremiah, "Return, thou backsliding Israel... for I am merciful" (Jer 3:12). In these prophets, returning is relational: a people coming home to the God who has not stopped loving them.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/repent
blocks.body:
In first-century Judea "repent" was also political. Israel faced a choice between paths: armed revolt against Rome, or Jesus' way of loving enemies and trusting God.

The historian Josephus records himself telling a rebel leader to "repent and trust" him, meaning: abandon your plan and follow mine. Jesus' "Repent, and believe" (Mark 1:15) would have sounded similarly concrete: turn from the agenda you are on, and trust me. In Luke 13:1-5 Jesus links failure to repent with literal violent destruction ("ye shall all likewise perish").

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/repent
blocks.body: N. T. Wright draws attention to Josephus' use of "repent and believe in me" and argues that Jesus' summons was not mainly a call to private moral regret but a call to Israel to abandon its revolutionary path and to trust Jesus' way of being God's people.

citations.ref: Jesus and the Victory of God (on repentance and belief)

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/repent
blocks.body:
"Repent" is often heard as "feel terrible about yourself so God will be willing to forgive you". That puts the turning before the mercy, as if repentance were a fee.

In Jesus' stories the order is reversed. The shepherd carries the sheep home (Luke 15:5), and the father runs to the son before the son can finish his speech (Luke 15:20). Repentance is being found and agreeing to come home. Sorrow may come with it, but the heart of it is a change of direction and a change of mind about who the Father is.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/repent
blocks.body:
Metanoia is a change of mind about God. Many people turn from a God they imagine to be angry and distant. Jesus says: the kingdom is at hand; the Father is nearer and kinder than you thought. Turn around.

Repentance is therefore the doorway into communion, not the price of it. "The goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance" (Rom 2:4).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/eternal-life
blocks.body:
*Aiōnios* is the adjective from *aiōn*, "age". In the Greek Old Testament it renders Hebrew *ʿôlām*, a word for a long, hidden or unending time.

Daniel 12:2 is the key background: "many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life (*ḥayyê ʿôlām*)". Jewish teachers divided history into "this age" and "the age to come". The life of the age to come was resurrection life in God's renewed world.

So *zōē aiōnios* is first a statement about the quality and source of life (the age to come, God's own life) and then about its duration.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/eternal-life
blocks.body:
When the rich man asked "what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?" (Mark 10:17), he was asking how to have a share in the age to come, the coming kingdom. Jesus' answer turns to the kingdom (Mark 10:23-25), and he promises "in the world to come eternal life" (Mark 10:30).

John's Gospel adds the surprise that this life is available now: whoever hears and trusts "hath everlasting life... and is passed from death unto life" (John 5:24).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/eternal-life
blocks.body:
Eternal life is often heard as "going to heaven forever after death", a reward for having the correct status. That turns life into a location and a duration.

Jesus defines it as knowing the Father and the Son (John 17:3). "Know" in Hebrew thought is intimate and personal (Gen 4:1). Eternal life is participation in the life the Father and Son share in the Spirit, starting now and raised up fully at the resurrection.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/eternal-life
blocks.body: N. T. Wright argues that Christian hope is not mainly about going to heaven when you die but about resurrection and new creation, "life after life after death". He reads *zōē aiōnios* as the life of the coming age, which God's people begin to taste in the present.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/eternal-life
blocks.body:
Eternal life is the Trinity's own life opened to us. The Son came that we might "have life, and... have it more abundantly" (John 10:10). It is not a thing he hands over; it is himself, shared (1 John 5:11-12).

That means eternal life is relational from first to last: union with Christ, sonship before the Father, communion in the Spirit.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/gehenna
blocks.body:
*Geenna* is the Greek spelling of Hebrew *gê hinnōm*, "Valley of (the son of) Hinnom", a ravine on Jerusalem's south-west side. Kings Ahaz and Manasseh burned children there to Molech at Tophet (2 Chr 28:3; 33:6). Josiah defiled the site to end the practice (2 Kgs 23:10).

Jeremiah announced that the valley would be renamed "the valley of slaughter", filled with the corpses of Jerusalem's people when the city fell (Jer 7:31-34; 19:6). Isaiah's last verse pictures the carcasses of rebels where "their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched" (Isa 66:24), the phrase Jesus quotes in Mark 9:48.

In later Jewish writings Gehinnom also became a name for the place of judgement after death. The popular claim that it was a constantly burning rubbish dump is not attested before medieval commentators and should be held loosely.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/gehenna
blocks.body:
Eleven of the twelve New Testament uses are in Jesus' mouth, and most are addressed to Jewish hearers, often disciples or religious leaders, not to pagans. To Jerusalemites the word called up a real valley with a terrible history and Jeremiah's promise of corpses there after a siege.

When Jesus asks the scribes and Pharisees "how can ye escape the damnation of Gehenna?" he follows at once with "All these things shall come upon this generation" (Matt 23:33-36).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/gehenna
blocks.body:
How to read Gehenna is genuinely disputed. Three main readings:

- **Traditional:** Gehenna is the final place of punishment after the last judgement, often understood as everlasting conscious torment. This has been the majority view in Western theology since Augustine (City of God, book 21).
- **Restorative or conditional readings:** fire in Scripture often purifies (Mal 3:2-3; 1 Cor 3:13-15), and the image of corpses consumed (Isa 66:24) can point to destruction rather than endless torment. Supporters include several patristic writers and many modern authors.
- **Partial-preterist (minority):** many Gehenna sayings warned Jesus' own generation that rejecting his way would end in the very scene Jeremiah described: the slaughter of Jerusalem and the valleys filled with bodies, fulfilled in the Roman siege of AD 70. This reading need not deny a final judgement; it argues that Jesus' immediate warnings had a near, historical target.

Readers should notice that the word "hell" in English Bibles merges several distinct terms (*Sheol*, *Hades*, *Tartarus*, *Gehenna*).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/gehenna
blocks.body: N. T. Wright reads many of Jesus' warnings of judgement, including Gehenna sayings, as first of all prophetic warnings to Israel about the coming national disaster if it refused his way of peace, a disaster that fell in the Roman war of AD 66-70.

citations.ref: Jesus and the Victory of God (on Jesus' warnings of judgement)

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/gehenna
blocks.body: Josephus describes how, during the Roman siege, the dead of Jerusalem were thrown over the walls into the valleys around the city in huge numbers. Partial-preterist interpreters read this as the grim historical fulfilment of Jeremiah's "valley of slaughter" (Jer 7:32) that stands behind Jesus' Gehenna sayings.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/gehenna
blocks.body:
Jesus' warnings are real, and they are the warnings of a Father's Son who weeps over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41-44). Gehenna names where the path of violence and idolatry ends: the valley where Israel once burned its own children. The God revealed in Jesus is the opposite of Molech.

Read through Jesus, judgement is God's refusal to let evil have the last word, not the Father's desire to torment his children. Whatever one concludes about the last things, the app reads these warnings as love: "turn, before the road you are on destroys you".

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/son-of-man
blocks.body:
In Hebrew and Aramaic "son of" expresses belonging to a class, so "son of man" (*ben-ʾādām*, *bar ʾĕnāš*) means "a human being". Psalm 8:4 uses it this way, and God addresses Ezekiel more than ninety times as "son of man", stressing his frailty before God (Ezek 2:1).

Daniel 7 gives the phrase a new weight. After four beasts (pagan empires), "one like a son of man" comes with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days and is given "dominion, and glory, and a kingdom" that will not pass away (Dan 7:13-14). The human figure stands for "the saints of the most High" and is also their royal representative (Dan 7:18, 27).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/son-of-man
blocks.body: The title was ambiguous on purpose. Sometimes it sounded like "this man" or "someone like me" (Matt 8:20). But at his trial Jesus joins Daniel 7:13 to Psalm 110:1: "ye shall see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven" (Mark 14:62). The high priest tore his robes. He heard a claim to share God's throne and to be vindicated over the court that was judging him.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/son-of-man
blocks.body:
Many readers assume "Son of Man" stresses Jesus' humanity and "Son of God" his divinity. In Daniel 7 the reverse is nearer the truth: the son-of-man figure rides the clouds, which in the Hebrew Bible is something God does (Ps 104:3; Isa 19:1), and receives worldwide service.

A second dispute concerns direction. Popular readings take "coming with the clouds" as Jesus' descent to earth at the end of history. In Daniel the figure comes *to* the Ancient of Days, upward, to be enthroned. Many scholars, and partial-preterist interpreters, read Mark 14:62 and Matt 24:30 first as Jesus' vindication and enthronement, made visible in the resurrection, ascension and the judgement on the Temple in AD 70. Others hold that these texts refer mainly to the Second Coming.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/son-of-man
blocks.body: N. T. Wright argues that "coming on the clouds" in Daniel 7 describes vindication and exaltation, not a downward journey. Jesus used it to say that God would vindicate him after his suffering, and that the destruction of the Temple would show him to be in the right.

citations.ref: Jesus and the Victory of God (on Daniel 7 and Mark 14:62)

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/son-of-man
blocks.body: Michael Heiser reads Daniel 7 against the Hebrew Bible's "two powers" pattern: the cloud-rider is a second divine figure alongside the Ancient of Days. On this reading, Jesus' use of the title was a claim to be that second figure, which explains the charge of blasphemy.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/son-of-man
blocks.body:
The Son of Man is the true human, Adam as he was meant to be, standing before the Father on behalf of all humanity. He takes our frail flesh (Ezekiel's "son of man") and carries it into the Father's presence (Daniel's "son of man").

The early church put the logic simply: what is not assumed is not healed.Because the Son became fully human, our humanity is now seated with the Father in him (Eph 2:6). The title is a promise of restored union, not only a claim of rank.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/son-of-man
blocks.body: Gregory of Nazianzus argued against Apollinarius that Christ took a complete human nature, including a human mind, because "that which he has not assumed he has not healed".

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/take-up-your-cross
blocks.body:
Crucifixion was Rome's punishment for slaves, bandits and rebels. It was public and shaming. The condemned often carried the crossbeam (*patibulum*) to the place of execution (John 19:17). After the revolt led by Judas the Galilean and other uprisings, Galileans knew what crosses along the roads meant: this is what happens to those who resist Caesar.

*Stauros* means an upright stake or cross. The word itself carried no religious meaning before Jesus.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/take-up-your-cross
blocks.body:
Jesus said this immediately after Peter called him the Messiah and then rebuked him for predicting his suffering (Mark 8:29-34). Hearers expected the Messiah to defeat Rome. Jesus tells them that his kingdom will come by suffering at Rome's hands, and that following him means walking toward the same fate, not toward the throne they imagined.

"Take up your cross" would have sounded shocking, even absurd: like telling people today to walk to their own execution.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/take-up-your-cross
blocks.body:
"My cross to bear" is often used for any burden: an illness, a difficult relative. That domesticates the saying. Jesus is not describing unchosen hardship but a chosen way of life: laying down power, status and self-protection for love of God and neighbour.

The opposite error treats cross-bearing as self-hatred or as earning God's favour through suffering. Jesus calls it the way to find life (Mark 8:35). It is the way the Son himself walks, trusting his Father.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/take-up-your-cross
blocks.body:
The cross is not first something God demanded of Jesus to satisfy wrath; it is the shape of God's own love, the Son giving himself for the world (Gal 2:20; Phil 2:5-8). On the cross the powers that rule by violence are exposed and defeated (Col 2:15).

To take up the cross is to share the Son's life: to love enemies, to refuse retaliation, to give ourselves away. It is participation in Christ, not imitation from a distance. And it ends in resurrection.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/born-from-above
blocks.body:
*Anōthen* normally means "from above" and can also mean "from the beginning" or "again". Elsewhere in John it clearly means "from above": "He that cometh from above is above all" (John 3:31); "except it were given thee from above" (John 19:11); the seamless robe woven "from the top" (John 19:23).

Nicodemus hears "again" and asks how a grown man can re-enter his mother's womb (John 3:4). Jesus' answer, "born of water and of the Spirit", draws on Ezekiel's promise that God will sprinkle clean water, give a new heart and put his Spirit within his people (Ezek 36:25-27).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/born-from-above
blocks.body:
Nicodemus was a Pharisee and "a ruler of the Jews" (John 3:1), a member of the council. As a Jew he would assume that birth into Abraham's family already gave a share in the kingdom. Jesus says entry depends on a birth from God, the very thing John's prologue described: "born, not of blood... but of God" (John 1:13).

Jesus chides him: "Art thou a master of Israel, and knowest not these things?" (John 3:10). Ezekiel 36-37 should have prepared him.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/born-from-above
blocks.body:
"Born again" often names a dateable conversion experience or a category of Christian. That is not wrong, but it can turn the new birth into something we produce by a decision.

Jesus' point is the source: from above, of the Spirit, who "bloweth where it listeth" (John 3:8). Birth is not something a baby achieves. The Father gives it, as gift, through the Son lifted up (John 3:14-16).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/born-from-above
blocks.body: Athanasius taught that the Word became human so that humans could share in the divine life: "He was made man that we might be made God". The new birth from above, on this reading, is our sharing by grace in the Son's own sonship.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/born-from-above
blocks.body:
To be born from above is to be brought into the Son's relationship with the Father. Those who receive him are given "power to become the sons of God" (John 1:12).

The new birth is adoption made real by the Spirit. It is not a change of legal file but a change of family and of life: the life of the age to come entering us now.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/i-am
blocks.body:
In Greek, *egō eimi* can simply mean "It's me" or "I am he" (John 9:9). Used without a predicate, it echoes the Greek Old Testament. At the burning bush God says *egō eimi ho ōn*, "I am the one who is" (Exod 3:14 LXX). In Isaiah God repeatedly says *egō eimi* (Hebrew *ʾănî hûʾ*, "I am he"): "that ye may know and believe me, and understand that I am he" (Isa 43:10; compare 41:4; 46:4).

The seven image sayings in John are: bread of life (6:35), light of the world (8:12), door (10:7), good shepherd (10:11), resurrection and life (11:25), way, truth and life (14:6), true vine (15:1).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/i-am
blocks.body:
The reactions in John show how the absolute sayings were heard. "Before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58) leads at once to an attempt to stone him. When the arresting party says they seek Jesus of Nazareth and he answers "I am", they fall to the ground (John 18:5-6).

In Mark, when Jesus walks on the sea he says "Be of good cheer: it is I (*egō eimi*); be not afraid" (Mark 6:50). Jewish hearers knew that it is God who "treadeth upon the waves of the sea" (Job 9:8).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/i-am
blocks.body:
The "I am" sayings are sometimes read as a list of separate religious services Jesus provides: bread for hunger, light for guidance, and so on. Each image is instead a claim that what Israel received from God (manna, the pillar of fire, the shepherd of Psalm 23, the vine of Israel) is now present in Jesus himself.

The point is not "Jesus supplies things" but "in Jesus, God is here".

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/i-am
blocks.body:
"I am" is the Father's name spoken by the Son. Jesus can speak it because he and the Father are one (John 10:30), and "he that hath seen me hath seen the Father" (John 14:9).

This is the root of "Jesus is perfect theology": we do not need to look behind Jesus for a different God. Whatever God is, he is as Jesus is. And each "I am" is an invitation: eat, come to the light, enter, be carried, live, abide.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/amen-amen
blocks.body:
*Amen* comes from the Hebrew root *ʾ-m-n*, "to be firm, reliable" (the root of *ʾĕmûnāh*, faithfulness). In the Hebrew Bible the people answer "Amen" to curses, blessings and prayers, meaning "so be it, it is firm" (Deut 27:15-26; Neh 8:6). Doubled "Amen, amen" appears as a response in Num 5:22 and Neh 8:6.

Isaiah 65:16 calls God "the God of amen" (KJV "the God of truth"). Revelation 3:14 calls Christ "the Amen, the faithful and true witness".

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/amen-amen
blocks.body:
A teacher of the time would usually ground his teaching in Scripture or in earlier rabbis ("Rabbi so-and-so said..."). Jesus opens with his own guarantee: "Amen, I say to you". Matthew notes the crowds' reaction: "he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes" (Matt 7:29).

The Gospels kept the Hebrew-Aramaic word in Greek, as with *abba*, which suggests it was remembered as characteristic of Jesus' voice.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/amen-amen
blocks.body: It is easy to treat "verily, verily" as an archaic flourish and skip past it. It is better read as a signal: what follows is something Jesus personally stakes his trustworthiness on, often a surprising promise ("He that heareth my word... hath everlasting life", John 5:24).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/amen-amen
blocks.body:
Jesus does not merely say amen; he *is* the Amen (Rev 3:14). "All the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen" (2 Cor 1:20).

The Father's faithfulness has a human face. When Jesus says "Amen" before speaking, he invites us to lean our whole weight on his words, because they are the Father's own.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/blessed
blocks.body:
*Makarios* renders Hebrew *ʾashrê* (from a root about walking straight or going forward), as in "Blessed (*ʾashrê*) is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly" (Ps 1:1) and "Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven" (Ps 32:1).

It is different from *barukh* / *eulogētos*, the word for blessing that God or a priest pronounces. *Makarios* is an exclamation: "Oh the happiness of...", "How well off are...". In Greek writing it could describe the gods' carefree state.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/blessed
blocks.body:
In an honour/shame culture, the poor, the grieving, the persecuted and the meek were not envied. Many assumed suffering signalled God's displeasure (John 9:2).

Jesus reverses the scale. Luke's version is blunter: "Blessed be ye poor... Woe unto you that are rich" (Luke 6:20, 24). The hearers would recognise the prophetic pattern of Isaiah 61:1-3: good news to the poor, comfort to those who mourn. The beatitudes announce that this promised reversal has begun.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/blessed
blocks.body:
The beatitudes are often read as entrance requirements: become poor in spirit, mourn enough, be meek, and then you will qualify for the kingdom.

They are announcements before they are instructions. Jesus is not telling the crowd how to earn blessing; he is declaring that the people who seemed furthest from God's favour are the very ones the kingdom is arriving for.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/blessed
blocks.body:
The beatitudes are the Father's heart turned toward the overlooked. Jesus lives them before he teaches them: he is the meek one, the mourner, the persecuted peacemaker.

"Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God" (Matt 5:9). The blessed life is the family likeness of the Father's children, sharing the Son's way in the world.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/the-father-who-sent-me
blocks.body:
Jewish law and custom recognised the *shaliach*, an authorised agent. A later rabbinic saying puts it: "a man's agent is like himself" (Mishnah Berakhot 5:5). What the agent did in the sender's name counted as the sender's act.

John uses two verbs for sending, *pempō* and *apostellō* (the root of "apostle"), almost interchangeably. More than forty times the Father is described as sending the Son.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/the-father-who-sent-me
blocks.body: Hearers would understand the claim of agency: to dishonour the agent is to dishonour the sender (John 5:23). But Jesus goes further than any agent. He says he and the Father are one (10:30), that the Father is in him and he in the Father (14:10), and that he was with the Father "before the world was" (17:5). This is why his opponents accuse him of "making himself equal with God" (5:18).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/the-father-who-sent-me
blocks.body: Some preaching sets the Son against the Father: a loving Son persuading or appeasing a reluctant, angry Father. John's language rules this out. The Father *sent* the Son because he "so loved the world" (John 3:16). The Son does "always those things that please him" (8:29). There is no gap between them to be bridged.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/the-father-who-sent-me
blocks.body:
"He that hath seen me hath seen the Father" (John 14:9). This is the heart of reading the Bible through Jesus: the Son is the Father's self-expression, "the express image of his person" (Heb 1:3).

The sending continues: "as my Father hath sent me, even so send I you" (John 20:21). The church is drawn into the Son's mission and the Son's relationship, sent from the Father's love into the world.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/it-is-finished
blocks.body:
*Tetelestai* is the perfect passive of *teleō*, "to bring to an end, complete, carry out". The perfect tense stresses a completed act with lasting results: it has been accomplished and stands accomplished.

John prepares for the word. Jesus' food is "to finish (*teleiōsō*) his work" (John 4:34). He loved his own "unto the end" (*eis telos*, 13:1). He prays, "I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do" (17:4). Just before dying, "knowing that all things were now accomplished (*tetelestai*)" he says "I thirst" (19:28).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/it-is-finished
blocks.body: John's readers knew Genesis: "Thus the heavens and the earth were finished... And on the seventh day God ended his work" (Gen 2:1-2, LXX *synetelesthēsan*). Jesus dies on the sixth day, Friday, and rests in the tomb on the Sabbath. John's Gospel opens "In the beginning" and frames the cross as the completion of God's work of making humanity.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/it-is-finished
blocks.body:
A widespread sermon illustration says *tetelestai* was written on receipts to mean "paid in full", so Jesus was declaring a debt paid to God.

The evidence is thinner than often claimed. *Teleō* can mean "to pay" (Matt 17:24; Rom 13:6), and forms of it appear in papyrus receipts, but John's own usage points to completion of a work, not settlement of an account. The commercial reading is possible as a secondary echo; making it the main meaning imports a later legal frame into John.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/it-is-finished
blocks.body:
**How the legal reading arose.** Anselm (Cur Deus Homo, book 1, chs. 11-13) framed sin as robbing God of honour, a debt that must be repaid by satisfaction. The Reformers sharpened this into penal terms: Calvin presented Christ as bearing in our place the punishment God's justice required (Institutes 2.16). Read through that frame, "It is finished" became "the penalty is paid".

The relational authors read it differently. In John, what is finished is the Son's work of revealing the Father and loving his own "to the end": the new creation of humanity and the defeat of the ruler of this world (John 12:31).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/it-is-finished
blocks.body: Gustaf Aulén argued that the "classic" view of the atonement in the early church was a drama of victory: Christ fights and triumphs over the powers of sin, death and the devil. On this reading the cross is the decisive battle won, not a transaction with the Father.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/it-is-finished
blocks.body:
What is finished is the Son's perfect "yes" to the Father in our humanity, sustained even into death. Love has gone all the way; nothing in our condition remains untouched by him.

The old creation's story is completed on the sixth day, and on the first day of the new week the risen Jesus breathes his Spirit into his disciples (John 20:22), as God breathed into Adam. The cross finishes the work; resurrection begins the new creation.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/this-generation
blocks.body:
*Genea* means a generation: the people living at one time, or the span of a lifetime (about thirty to forty years). It renders Hebrew *dôr*.

In the Gospels "this generation" consistently means Jesus' contemporaries: "whereunto shall I liken this generation?" (Matt 11:16); "an evil and adulterous generation" (12:39); "All these things shall come upon this generation" (23:36). The phrase echoes Moses' "perverse and crooked generation" (Deut 32:5) and the wilderness generation that did not enter the land (Ps 95:10).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/this-generation
blocks.body:
The disciples' question that triggers the prophecy is about the Temple: "There shall not be left here one stone upon another... Tell us, when shall these things be?" (Matt 24:2-3; Mark 13:2-4). Jesus' hearers would take "this generation" in its ordinary sense: people now alive.

Within forty years, Roman armies besieged Jerusalem and burned the Temple (AD 70). Eusebius reports that Jerusalem's Christians, warned beforehand, fled the city to Pella before the war.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/this-generation
blocks.body:
Readings differ sharply:

- **Partial preterist (minority, but growing):** "all these things" in Matt 24:4-34 were fulfilled in the generation that heard Jesus, culminating in AD 70. The "coming of the Son of Man" in that passage is prophetic language for Christ's vindication and judgement on the old order (compare Isa 19:1). The final, bodily Second Coming is taught elsewhere and remains future.
- **Futurist:** *genea* means "race" (the Jewish people) or "the generation that sees these signs", so the prophecy awaits the end of history.
- **Some critical scholars:** Jesus expected the end of the world within a generation and was mistaken.

Partial preterism takes *genea* in its normal Gospel sense and avoids the conclusion that Jesus was wrong.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/this-generation
blocks.body: Gary DeMar argues that "this generation" in Matthew 24:34 must mean Jesus' contemporaries, and that the signs in Matthew 24 (false messiahs, wars, the gospel preached to the known world, the abomination, flight from Judea) were fulfilled before and during the Jewish War, culminating in the Temple's destruction in AD 70.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/this-generation
blocks.body: J. Marcellus Kik divided Matthew 24 at verse 35: verses before it describe the fall of Jerusalem within "this generation", and the following verses turn to the final coming of Christ, whose day and hour no one knows.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/this-generation
blocks.body:
Taking "this generation" at face value lets Jesus be a true prophet: what he said would happen within a lifetime did happen. It also frees the church from reading every newspaper as a sign of the end.

The judgement on the Temple was the end of an age (the old covenant order), and with it the Father's house was opened to all nations in the Son. History since then is the time of the kingdom's growth, not of anxious waiting for collapse.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/end-of-the-age
blocks.body:
*Synteleia* means completion or consummation. *Aiōn* means "age", not "world" (*kosmos*); the KJV's "end of the world" has misled many readers.

Jewish writings spoke of "this age" and "the age to come" (compare Matt 12:32). Hebrews uses the same phrase for the time of Christ's sacrifice: "now once in the end of the world (*synteleia tōn aiōnōn*) hath he appeared" (Heb 9:26). Paul says the ends of the ages have come upon his readers (1 Cor 10:11).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/end-of-the-age
blocks.body: The disciples ask, "when shall these things be? and what shall be the sign of thy coming, and of the end of the age?" (Matt 24:3), immediately after Jesus predicts the Temple's destruction. For Jews, the Temple was the centre of the world; its destruction would be heard as the end of an era, the old order passing away.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/end-of-the-age
blocks.body:
- **Traditional and futurist reading (majority):** "the end of the age" refers to the end of history, the final judgement and Christ's return, in all its uses.
- **Partial preterist (minority):** at least in Matt 24:3, the end of the age is the end of the Mosaic covenant age, marked by the Temple's fall in AD 70 (compare Heb 8:13, "that which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away"). Some partial preterists apply this to the harvest parables of Matt 13 as well; others keep those for the final judgement.

Both readings agree that Christ promises his presence "unto the end of the age" (Matt 28:20).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/end-of-the-age
blocks.body: Kenneth Gentry reads Matthew 24:1-34 as fulfilled in AD 70 and holds, as a postmillennialist, that the gospel will progressively win the nations before Christ's final return.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/end-of-the-age
blocks.body:
Whether one end is in view or two, the comfort of Jesus' last words stands: "lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the age" (Matt 28:20). The risen Son has all authority, and his presence is the guarantee of the mission.

The app's partial-preterist reading sees AD 70 as a hinge: the old age of Temple and sacrifice closing, the age of the Son and Spirit opening to the nations, and the kingdom growing toward the final renewal of all things.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/my-peace
blocks.body:
*Shalom* is broader than the absence of conflict. It means completeness, health, prosperity and right relationship, between people and with God. The priestly blessing ends "The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace" (Num 6:26). The Messiah is "the Prince of Peace" (Isa 9:6), and "the chastisement of our peace was upon him" (Isa 53:5).

"Shalom" was also the everyday greeting and farewell, as it still is.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/my-peace
blocks.body:
The disciples lived under the *Pax Romana*, the Roman peace secured by legions and crosses. Jesus contrasts his gift: "not as the world giveth, give I unto you" (John 14:27).

After Easter, the disciples had abandoned him. They were behind locked doors "for fear of the Jews" (John 20:19). Jesus' first word is not rebuke but "Peace be unto you", repeated, with the wounds shown. Hearers would understand: the broken relationship is restored by him.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/my-peace
blocks.body:
Peace is often reduced to an inner calm we work up through technique. Jesus' peace is a gift, "my peace", and it comes with his presence and his wounds. It holds even where "in the world ye shall have tribulation" (John 16:33).

It is also communal and public: shalom is what the kingdom brings to relationships, not only to individual feelings.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/my-peace
blocks.body:
Jesus gives the peace he has always shared with the Father. Reconciliation is not God being talked out of anger; it is "God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself" (2 Cor 5:19).

The risen Son's "Peace be unto you" to deserters is the gospel in miniature: the Father's welcome extended through the Son, sealed by the Spirit he breathes on them.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/abide-in-me
blocks.body:
*Menō* means to stay, remain, dwell, continue. John uses it about forty times, more than any other New Testament writer. The related noun *monē* appears in "In my Father's house are many mansions (*monai*, dwelling places)" (John 14:2) and "we will come unto him, and make our abode (*monē*) with him" (14:23).

The vine was a classic image for Israel: God brought a vine out of Egypt and planted it (Ps 80:8), but the vineyard produced wild grapes (Isa 5:1-7). A golden vine decorated the entrance of Herod's Temple.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/abide-in-me
blocks.body:
The disciples would hear "I am the true vine" (John 15:1) as a claim to be true Israel, the faithful vine God always wanted. To be part of God's people is now to be joined to Jesus.

Vinedressers pruned hard after harvest and cut away dead wood for burning. Galileans knew how utterly a branch depends on the stock.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/abide-in-me
blocks.body:
"Abide" is often heard as a demanding spiritual discipline: try harder to stay close to Jesus or you will be cut off. But a branch does not abide by effort. It simply stays where it has been joined.

Jesus' first word is that the disciples are already clean and already in him (John 15:3). Abiding is resting in a union he has made, and "continue ye in my love" (15:9) is an invitation, not a threat.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/abide-in-me
blocks.body:
The vine is the Trinity's life flowing into us. "As the Father hath loved me, so have I loved you" (John 15:9). The love the Father has for the Son is the love the Son shares with his branches.

This is union with Christ in its simplest form. Fruit (love, joy, peace) is not produced to earn the union; it grows because the union is real.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/light-of-the-world
blocks.body:
John sets the saying during or just after Tabernacles (John 7:2, 37; 8:12). The Mishnah describes huge golden lamps lit in the Court of the Women during the feast, and says there was no courtyard in Jerusalem that was not lit by them. The feast remembered the pillar of fire in the wilderness (Exod 13:21).

Prophets promised light for the nations through God's servant: "I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles" (Isa 49:6). Zechariah's vision of the last day, read at Tabernacles, says "at evening time it shall be light" (Zech 14:7).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/light-of-the-world
blocks.body: Standing in the Temple, perhaps under the very lamps, Jesus claims to be what they symbolised: the pillar of God's presence leading his people, and the light promised to the Gentiles. The next chapter shows it concretely: he gives sight to a man born blind (John 9:5-7).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/light-of-the-world
blocks.body:
Light is sometimes read only as information: Jesus gives correct doctrine. In John, light is life: "In him was life; and the life was the light of men" (John 1:4). It is the presence of God that makes people alive and lets them see.

And "Ye are the light of the world" (Matt 5:14) is not a burden to generate light; it is the result of being lit by him.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/light-of-the-world
blocks.body:
Light reveals what God is like. The Father is "light, and in him is no darkness at all" (1 John 1:5), and the Son is that light shining in our darkness (John 1:5).

Read through Jesus, nothing in God is dark or threatening. The light that "lighteth every man" (John 1:9) is the Father's self-giving shining in the Son, and the church shares it with the nations.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/living-water
blocks.body:
In Hebrew, *mayim ḥayyîm*, "living water", is the ordinary term for flowing water from a spring or stream, as opposed to still water in a cistern. Jewish purity law required living water for certain cleansings (Lev 14:5; 15:13).

The prophets use it for God himself: Israel "have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns" (Jer 2:13; 17:13). Ezekiel sees a river flowing from the Temple that makes the Dead Sea fresh (Ezek 47:1-12), and Zechariah says "living waters shall go out from Jerusalem" (Zech 14:8).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/living-water
blocks.body:
The Samaritan woman hears "living water" literally: running water, better than the well's (John 4:11). She came at noon, likely avoiding other women.

At Tabernacles, priests carried water daily from the Pool of Siloam and poured it at the altar, with Isaiah 12:3 sung: "with joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation". On the last, great day Jesus stands and calls the thirsty to himself (John 7:37). John adds: "this spake he of the Spirit" (7:39).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/living-water
blocks.body: Living water is sometimes reduced to a feeling of satisfaction or to religious knowledge. John identifies it with the Spirit, given by the glorified Son (John 7:39). It is God's own life flowing into people and out of them "rivers of living water" (7:38).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/living-water
blocks.body:
Jesus seeks out a woman who is a Samaritan, a woman, and a person with a complicated history, and offers her the Spirit before she has asked. That is the Father's way: he "seeketh such to worship him" (John 4:23).

The Spirit is the life the Father and Son share, now poured out. It is never stagnant, never a cistern we have to keep full. It flows.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/bread-of-life
blocks.body:
John sets the feeding and discourse near Passover (John 6:4). The crowd quotes Psalm 78:24, "He gave them bread from heaven to eat" (John 6:31), recalling the manna (Exod 16).

Some Jewish expectation held that the Messiah, like a second Moses, would bring manna again. Bread (*leḥem*) was the main food of the poor; "bread" could stand for food and life itself. Deuteronomy 8:3 teaches that "man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD".

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/bread-of-life
blocks.body: The crowd wanted a Moses-like king who would keep feeding them (John 6:15, 26). Jesus says the Father, not Moses, gives the true bread, and that bread is Jesus himself. When he adds that they must eat his flesh and drink his blood (6:53), many disciples leave. To Jewish ears, drinking blood was forbidden (Lev 17:10-14). The saying offended because it was so physical.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/bread-of-life
blocks.body: Readers sometimes split this chapter into rival camps: either it is all about the Lord's Supper, or it is only a metaphor for believing. John holds both together: "he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst" (John 6:35), and also real eating and drinking of the Son's self-giving.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/bread-of-life
blocks.body:
The Father gives the Son as food. The language of eating is the language of union: "He that eateth my flesh... dwelleth in me, and I in him" (John 6:56).

The Son lives "by the Father", and those who feed on him live by him (6:57). The table is the place where the Trinity's life is shared with hungry people, which is why Jesus kept eating with sinners.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/good-shepherd
blocks.body:
In the ancient Near East, "shepherd" was a common title for kings. Israel's ideal king David had been a shepherd. Psalm 23 confesses "The LORD is my shepherd".

Ezekiel 34 is the key text. God condemns the shepherds (leaders) of Israel who fed themselves and not the flock, and promises: "I, even I, will both search my sheep, and seek them out... I will seek that which was lost" (Ezek 34:11, 16). He also promises "one shepherd... my servant David" (34:23).

*Kalos* means good, beautiful, noble: the shepherd as he truly ought to be.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/good-shepherd
blocks.body:
The discourse follows the healing of the man born blind, whom the Pharisees cast out (John 9:34). Jesus contrasts himself with thieves, robbers and hirelings (10:1, 12): the leaders who expelled a healed sheep.

Village shepherds in Palestine led their flocks, calling them by name; the sheep knew their voice (10:3-4). At night a shepherd might sleep across the entrance of the fold, becoming its door (10:7).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/good-shepherd
blocks.body:
The good shepherd is often pictured as gentle but passive. In John 10 he is the one who confronts wolves and robbers and lays down his life by his own authority (10:18). His goodness includes courage and power.

Another misreading makes the shepherd's death a payment to the owner of the sheep. In the image, the shepherd dies *for* the sheep against the wolf; the danger is the enemy, not the Father.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/good-shepherd
blocks.body:
In Ezekiel, God says "I myself will be the shepherd". In John, Jesus says "I am". The Father's promise to come and seek the lost is fulfilled in person by the Son.

"My sheep hear my voice, and I know them... My Father, which gave them me, is greater than all; and no man is able to pluck them out of my Father's hand. I and my Father are one" (John 10:27-30). The safety of the sheep lies in the union of Father and Son.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/follow-me
blocks.body:
In Jewish practice, students usually sought out a teacher to study Torah with. Jesus reverses this: he calls people himself. The closest Old Testament parallel is Elijah calling Elisha from his plough by throwing his mantle over him (1 Kgs 19:19-21). Jesus' demand is sharper: Elisha could kiss his parents goodbye; Jesus' would-be follower may not even bury his father first (Matt 8:21-22).

*Akoloutheō* means to go behind, accompany. Mark's "Come ye after me" (*deute opisō mou*, Mark 1:17) is the language of a servant walking behind a master.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/follow-me
blocks.body: Fishermen in Galilee ran family businesses; leaving the boat and the father (Mark 1:20) was an economic and social shock. Levi left a tax booth (Mark 2:14), which in an honour/shame culture marked him as a collaborator. Calling him publicly and then eating at his house was a statement that he belonged with Jesus.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/follow-me
blocks.body:
"Follow me" is sometimes reduced to "agree with my teachings" or "follow my example from a distance". Disciples in the Gospels walked, ate, slept and served with Jesus. The call was to a shared life.

It is also not a call to prove oneself worthy. Jesus calls tax collectors and fishermen before they have done anything.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/follow-me
blocks.body:
To follow Jesus is to be drawn into his relationship with the Father, going where he goes. The final "Follow thou me" is spoken to Peter after his denial and restoration (John 21:19-22): the call is renewed to the one who failed.

The Son does nothing except what he sees the Father doing (John 5:19). Following the Son means learning to live the same way, as beloved children.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/your-faith-has-saved-you
blocks.body:
*Sōzō* means to rescue, keep safe, heal, save. The same Greek phrase is translated "made thee whole" (Mark 5:34) and "saved thee" (Luke 7:50). English translations divide what the Greek holds together: bodily healing, social restoration and rescue before God.

*Pistis* is trust, faithfulness, reliance. In these stories it is shown by actions: pushing through a crowd, shouting despite rebukes, returning to give thanks.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/your-faith-has-saved-you
blocks.body:
Several of these people were excluded. A woman with a continual flow of blood was ritually unclean for twelve years (Lev 15:25-27). A blind beggar sat outside the city. A leper lived outside the village, and the one who returned was a Samaritan (Luke 17:16). The "woman in the city, which was a sinner" was shamed in a Pharisee's house (Luke 7:37).
