In each case Jesus publicly declares the person saved and whole, restoring them to the community. "Go in peace" sent them back into society with honour.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/your-faith-has-saved-you
blocks.body:
"Your faith" is sometimes heard as if the person's faith were the power that healed, so that failure to be healed means faith was too small.

In the stories, faith is turning toward Jesus with trust, often desperate, mixed and imperfect. The power is his ("virtue had gone out of him", Mark 5:30). Jesus credits their trust to honour them, not to burden others.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/your-faith-has-saved-you
blocks.body:
Salvation in the Gospels is whole-person restoration: body, relationships and standing before God. Jesus calls the healed woman "Daughter" (Mark 5:34), the only time he addresses anyone that way. She came for a cure and received a family.

That is what *sōzō* means through the lens of the Father's heart: being brought home and made whole.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/forgive
blocks.body:
*Aphiēmi* has a wide range: leave, let go, permit, release, cancel. The noun *aphesis* is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the Jubilee "release" (Lev 25:10) and that Jesus reads in Nazareth: "to preach deliverance (*aphesis*) to the captives... to set at liberty (*aphesis*) them that are bruised" (Luke 4:18).

In Aramaic, sin was commonly spoken of as debt (*ḥôbā*). Matthew's Lord's Prayer keeps the image: "forgive us our debts" (Matt 6:12); Luke has "sins" and "every one that is indebted to us" (Luke 11:4).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/forgive
blocks.body:
Debt was a crushing reality for Galilean peasants; debt slavery and land loss were common. Forgiveness of debts was concrete and economic as well as spiritual.

Forgiving sins was understood as God's prerogative, normally mediated through the Temple and its sacrifices. When Jesus says to a paralysed man, "Son, thy sins be forgiven thee" (Mark 2:5), the scribes object: "who can forgive sins but God only?" (2:7). Jesus bypasses the Temple system and acts as God does.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/forgive
blocks.body:
Forgiveness is often pictured as God deciding not to punish, after his justice has been satisfied. Jesus forgives freely, before any sacrifice, and from the cross itself: "Father, forgive them" (Luke 23:34).

Matthew 6:15 ("if ye forgive not... neither will your Father forgive") is sometimes read as a transaction. The parable of the unforgiving servant (Matt 18:23-35) shows the logic: the servant was forgiven first; refusing to pass it on means he never let the release change him.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/forgive
blocks.body:
To forgive is to release, to set free. The Father's forgiveness in Jesus is Jubilee for humanity: the debts cancelled, the captives let go, the family restored.

Forgiveness is not the end goal but the door to reconciliation and communion. It also becomes a family trait: we forgive because we share the Father's nature as his children (Eph 4:32).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/the-least-of-these
blocks.body:
Hospitality to strangers, care for the hungry and visiting prisoners were core Jewish duties (Isa 58:7; Job 31:16-20). Prisoners in the Roman world often relied on family and friends for food; without visitors they could starve.

*Elachistos* is the superlative of "small": the very least. Elsewhere in Matthew Jesus calls his disciples "these little ones" (Matt 10:42; 18:6) and calls those who do the Father's will "my brother, and sister" (12:50).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/the-least-of-these
blocks.body: Hearers would be startled that both groups are surprised. Neither the blessed nor the cursed knew they were dealing with the king. In honour/shame terms, the king identifies himself with the lowest in society, the people no one sought favour from.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/the-least-of-these
blocks.body:
Who are "the least of these my brethren"?

- **Universal reading:** any person in need. Jesus identifies with all who suffer. This reading has inspired centuries of Christian charity.
- **Disciple reading:** Jesus' brothers are his followers, especially messengers sent out with nothing (Matt 10:9-14, 40-42). The nations are judged by how they received Christ's messengers.

Both readings have strong defenders. Either way, care for the hungry, sick and imprisoned is how the nations meet Christ.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/the-least-of-these
blocks.body:
The Son of Man on his throne is not distant. He is hidden in the hungry and imprisoned, because he has joined himself to humanity at its lowest point.

The Father's children are recognised by the family likeness: mercy. The judgement here is not about religious credentials but about whether people have shared the Father's love with those he loves.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/the-narrow-gate
blocks.body:
The "two ways" is a familiar Jewish teaching form: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life" (Deut 30:19); "I set before you the way of life, and the way of death" (Jer 21:8); Psalm 1 contrasts the way of the righteous and of the ungodly. Early Christians continued it in the *Didache*, which opens "There are two ways, one of life and one of death".

*Stenos* means narrow, cramped. "Strait" in the KJV means narrow, not straight.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/the-narrow-gate
blocks.body:
In Matthew the saying comes at the end of the Sermon. The "narrow way" is the way just described: loving enemies, turning the other cheek, praying in secret, not storing up treasure, not judging. The "broad way" is the path most of Israel's leaders and many of the people were taking, including the road toward violent revolt.

In Luke, the saying answers the question "are there few that be saved?" (Luke 13:23), and Jesus turns it to the people at the table: many will come from east and west, and some who expected to be inside will be outside.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/the-narrow-gate
blocks.body:
Many read the saying as a statement about the final number of the saved: few, as against many lost. Others note that Jesus refuses to answer the "how many" question directly (Luke 13:23-24) and turns it into a summons.

A partial-preterist reading adds that "destruction" (*apōleia*) in Jesus' context included the historical catastrophe facing Israel if it chose the broad way of violence. Readers disagree about how much to stress this.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/the-narrow-gate
blocks.body:
The narrow gate is a person: "I am the door" (John 10:9). The way is narrow not because the Father is stingy but because it is the specific shape of the Son's life: self-giving love.

Jesus' warning is an invitation to life, spoken by someone who wants us through the gate. The Father's house has many dwelling places (John 14:2); the door is the Son.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/children-of-your-father
blocks.body:
In Hebrew idiom "son of X" means "having the quality of X": "sons of Belial" are worthless men, "son of peace" is a peaceable person (Luke 10:6), James and John are "sons of thunder" (Mark 3:17). To be a "son of the Father" is to share his character.

Israel was called God's son (Exod 4:22; Hos 11:1). In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus speaks of "your Father" about seventeen times, an unusually personal way of speaking for his time.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/children-of-your-father
blocks.body:
"Love your enemies" was startling in occupied Galilee. Roman soldiers could force civilians to carry gear a mile (Matt 5:41). Many hoped God would destroy Israel's enemies.

Jesus grounds the command not in a rule but in the Father's character: "he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good" (Matt 5:45). Luke's version: "he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil. Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful" (Luke 6:35-36).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/children-of-your-father
blocks.body:
"Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father... is perfect" (Matt 5:48) is often read as an impossible moral standard meant to drive us to despair. In context, "perfect" (*teleios*, complete, whole) refers to love that is not partial, love that includes enemies. Luke renders the same thought "merciful".

The call is not to flawless performance but to the Father's wholehearted kindness.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/children-of-your-father
blocks.body:
Sonship is the heart of the gospel. The Son shares his own relationship with the Father, and the Spirit makes us "the children of God" (Rom 8:14-16).

Children grow into a family likeness. Loving enemies is not a condition for adoption; it is what adoption looks like when the Father's life is at work in us. The God who makes his sun rise on the evil is the God revealed in Jesus praying for his executioners.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/talitha-koum
blocks.body:
*Ṭalyĕtāʾ* is Aramaic for "lamb" or "young one", used tenderly for a girl. *Qûm* is the command "rise"; the feminine form is *qûmî*. Greek manuscripts have both *koum* and *koumi*. Mark translates: "Damsel (*korasion*), I say unto thee, arise" (Mark 5:41).

Mark keeps several Aramaic words of Jesus: *Talitha koum*, *Ephphatha* (7:34), *Abba* (14:36), *Eloi, Eloi* (15:34). They read like remembered moments.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/talitha-koum
blocks.body:
Touching a corpse made a person ritually unclean for seven days (Num 19:11). Jesus has just been touched by a woman with a flow of blood (Mark 5:27). In both scenes, uncleanness does not flow to him; life flows from him.

Mourners had already gathered, as was customary, and they laughed at Jesus (Mark 5:38-40). Elijah and Elisha had raised children (1 Kgs 17; 2 Kgs 4) after prolonged prayer and effort. Jesus speaks two words.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/talitha-koum
blocks.body: Mark's Aramaic is sometimes treated as a magic formula. Mark translates it at once, as an ordinary sentence. The power is not in the words but in the person speaking them, the same voice that will call all the dead to rise (John 5:28-29).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/talitha-koum
blocks.body:
Death is not the Father's will for his children. Jesus treats death as an enemy and sleep (Mark 5:39), and he overcomes it by taking a child's hand.

This is Christus Victor in a single room: the Son entering the place of death, unafraid of defilement, and calling a daughter back to life and to her family's table ("he commanded that something should be given her to eat", Mark 5:43).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/eloi-eloi-lema-sabachthani
blocks.body:
Psalm 22:1 in Hebrew is *ʾēlî ʾēlî lāmâ ʿăzavtānî*. Mark's form is Aramaic: *Eloi* ("my God") and *sabachthani* from *šĕvaq*, "leave, abandon". Matthew has *Eli*, closer to Hebrew, which explains why bystanders thought he was calling Elijah (*Eliyyahu*) (Matt 27:47).

Jews often referred to a psalm by its first line. Psalm 22 moves from abandonment ("I am a worm", "they pierced my hands and my feet", "they part my garments") to deliverance: God "hath not despised nor abhorred the affliction of the afflicted; neither hath he hid his face from him" (Ps 22:24), and "all the ends of the world shall remember and turn unto the LORD" (22:27).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/eloi-eloi-lema-sabachthani
blocks.body: Hearers who knew the psalm would recognise the whole story. Mark's account echoes it repeatedly: the dividing of garments (Mark 15:24; Ps 22:18), the mocking and wagging heads (Mark 15:29; Ps 22:7). Immediately after Jesus dies, a Gentile centurion confesses "Truly this man was the Son of God" (Mark 15:39), the first fruit of "all the kindreds of the nations shall worship" (Ps 22:27).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/eloi-eloi-lema-sabachthani
blocks.body:
- **Penal reading:** at this moment the Father turned his face away from the Son, who bore the Father's wrath against sin in our place. This view is widespread in Reformed and evangelical preaching.
- **Psalm-22 and Trinitarian reading:** Jesus prays the psalm of the righteous sufferer, fully entering human experience of God-forsakenness, while the psalm itself says God did *not* hide his face (Ps 22:24). The Trinity is not divided. Jesus had said, "ye shall... leave me alone: and yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me" (John 16:32), and in Luke he dies saying "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit" (Luke 23:46; Ps 31:5).

The cry is real anguish, not play-acting. The question is whether it describes the Father abandoning the Son or the Son entering our abandonment with the Father.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/eloi-eloi-lema-sabachthani
blocks.body:
**How the legal reading arose.** Calvin, explaining the creed's "he descended into hell", taught that Christ on the cross endured in his soul the dreadful torments of a condemned and forsaken man, bearing the weight of divine severity in our place (Institutes 2.16.10-12). Later Protestant preaching often summarised this as the Father turning his face away. It reads the cry through a forensic frame of punishment transferred from sinners to Christ.

Relational authors read the cry as the Son's solidarity with humanity's alienation, healed from within, rather than as a breach in the Trinity.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/eloi-eloi-lema-sabachthani
blocks.body: Thomas F. Torrance taught the "vicarious humanity" of Christ: the Son assumed our fallen, alienated humanity and lived out, from within it, perfect trust and obedience toward the Father, healing our estrangement in his own person. The cry of dereliction belongs to that work of entering our God-forsakenness to bring it home.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/eloi-eloi-lema-sabachthani
blocks.body:
Jesus is perfect theology even here. If the Father and Son are one, the cross is not the Father against the Son but God in Christ, reconciling the world (2 Cor 5:19). The Son goes to the furthest place of human abandonment, so that no one who feels forsaken is beyond his reach.

He prays the psalm with us, from inside our darkness, and the psalm ends with the nations turning to the LORD. The centurion's confession is the first answer.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/lost
blocks.body:
*Apollymi* means to destroy (active) or to be lost, perish, be ruined (middle). The perfect participle *to apolōlos*, "that which has been lost", appears in Luke 15 and 19:10, echoing Ezekiel 34:16: "I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away".

The same word describes sheep that wander, a coin that drops, and a son who squanders everything. It can also mean "perishing" (John 3:16).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/lost
blocks.body:
Pharisees and scribes grumbled, "This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them" (Luke 15:2). In their framework, "sinners" (people who did not keep the law, or worked in disreputable trades) were to be avoided until they reformed.

Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector, was the classic "lost" case (Luke 19:1-10). Jesus invites himself to his house before Zacchaeus has done anything; Zacchaeus' generosity follows the welcome.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/lost
blocks.body: "Lost" is often heard as a label of condemnation: the lost versus the saved, outsiders under judgement. In Jesus' stories, "lost" is a word of value and belonging. A thing is only lost if someone owns it and misses it. The sheep is still the shepherd's sheep; the son is still the father's son ("this my son was dead... and is found", Luke 15:24).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/lost
blocks.body:
The lost belong to the Father before they are found. The initiative is entirely his: the shepherd searches, the woman sweeps, the father runs.

This is the gospel of adoption seen from the Father's side. Humanity was never an orphan in the Father's mind; we were lost children, and the Son came to bring us home.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/neighbour
blocks.body:
*Plēsion* is an adverb meaning "near", used as a noun: "the one near". It translates Hebrew *rēaʿ*, companion, fellow. Leviticus 19:18 commands "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself", and Leviticus 19:34 extends this to the resident alien: "thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt".

Jewish teachers debated whether "neighbour" included Gentiles, Samaritans, or only fellow Israelites in good standing.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/neighbour
blocks.body: The lawyer wants to "justify himself" (Luke 10:29): to define a boundary he can keep. Samaritans and Jews were bitter enemies; a Samaritan hero was a provocation. Jesus' final question changes the subject from "who qualifies for my love?" to "whose love made him a neighbour?" The lawyer cannot bring himself to say "the Samaritan" and answers "He that shewed mercy on him" (10:37).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/neighbour
blocks.body: The parable is often reduced to "help people in need". That is true, but it misses the edge: the hero is the despised outsider, and the religious professionals fail. The question is not only "will you help?" but "can you receive mercy from, and show mercy to, your enemy?"

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/neighbour
blocks.body:
Jesus himself is the neighbour who crossed the road to us, came near (*plēsion*) in the incarnation, and paid the cost of our healing.

To love the neighbour "as thyself" is to love from the security of being loved by the Father. There are no non-neighbours in the Father's family.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/hypocrite
blocks.body:
A *hypokritēs* was an actor in the Greek theatre, who wore masks to play roles. Sepphoris, a large city about four miles from Nazareth, was rebuilt under Herod Antipas during Jesus' youth; it later had a theatre, though its date is debated. Galileans would have known the word.

Jesus quotes Isaiah: "This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth... but have removed their heart far from me" (Isa 29:13; Matt 15:8).

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/hypocrite
blocks.body:
In an honour/shame culture, public piety earned public honour. Jesus describes people trumpeting their alms, praying on street corners and disfiguring their faces when fasting "that they may have glory of men" (Matt 6:2-5, 16). His verdict: "They have their reward", the honour they performed for.

The harshest "woes" (Matt 23) were spoken to leaders, not to the crowds, and often in public, which was itself a shaming act.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/hypocrite
blocks.body:
Matthew 23 has often been used to caricature all Pharisees, and sometimes Jews in general, as hypocrites. That is a serious misuse. Pharisees were a diverse lay renewal movement; Jesus shared many of their convictions (resurrection, the importance of the law, Matt 23:2-3), and some Pharisees were his friends (Luke 13:31; John 3:1).

Historians debate how far Matthew 23 reflects Jesus' own conflicts and how far it was sharpened by later conflicts between church and synagogue. Either way, the warning is aimed at religious insiders of every age, including Christians.

blocks.subject: entry:jesus_word/hypocrite
blocks.body:
Hypocrisy is living for the audience instead of the Father. Jesus' answer is not "try harder to be sincere" but "thy Father which seeth in secret" (Matt 6:4, 6, 18). Those who know they are loved in secret do not need to perform in public.

The Father does not want masks. He wants children who come as they are.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/sower
blocks.body:
In Galilee, sowing often came before ploughing: the farmer scattered seed broadcast across the field, including over the path trodden through it, and then ploughed it in. Seed on the path was exposed to birds. Much Galilean soil is a thin layer over limestone ("stony ground"), where seed sprouts fast and withers in the sun. Thorns grew from roots left in the soil.

A normal yield was perhaps sevenfold to tenfold; thirty, sixty and a hundredfold (compare Isaac's hundredfold, Gen 26:12) would sound like a miracle harvest, a sign of God's blessing in the age to come.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/sower
blocks.body:
Mark places the parable first in a block of seed parables (Mark 4:1-34). The story has four scenes, three failures and one success, with the success itself growing in three steps (thirty, sixty, a hundred). The pattern builds to a climax: the losses are real, but the harvest dwarfs them.

Between the parable and its explanation stands the quotation from Isaiah 6:9-10 about hearing without understanding (Mark 4:11-12). The parable is framed by the command "Hearken" (4:3) and "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear" (4:9).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/sower
blocks.body: N. T. Wright reads the sower as a story about Israel's history coming to its climax: God "sowing" his people again after exile (compare Jer 31:27; Hos 2:23), with the long-awaited harvest arriving in Jesus' ministry despite the many who reject it.

citations.ref: Jesus and the Victory of God (on the parable of the sower)

blocks.subject: entry:parable/sower
blocks.body:
The sower is extravagant. He throws seed everywhere, even on the path, because the Father's word is given generously, not rationed to the promising soil.

The parable does not tell hearers to inspect their soil anxiously. It tells them the kingdom will have its harvest. The Word himself is the seed that falls into the ground and dies and bears much fruit (John 12:24).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/growing-seed
blocks.body:
Farmers knew the rhythm of the season: sow after the early rains (October-November), wait through winter, harvest barley around Passover and wheat around Pentecost. Nothing a farmer did could make the grain grow faster.

"Putteth in the sickle, because the harvest is come" echoes Joel 3:13, a picture of God's decisive action at the end.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/growing-seed
blocks.body: The parable moves in three stages: sowing, secret growth, harvest. The centre is the growth, described in three steps: "first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear" (Mark 4:28). The Greek word for "by herself" is *automatē* (automatic), stressing that the growth does not depend on the sower.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/growing-seed
blocks.body:
The kingdom grows by the Father's power, not by human anxiety or control. That is good news for a postmillennial hope: the kingdom advances steadily and quietly, often unseen, toward a full harvest.

We are invited to sow and to sleep. The growth belongs to God.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/mustard-seed
blocks.body:
Black mustard (*Brassica nigra*) has tiny seeds and grows into a bushy annual plant two or three metres tall around the Sea of Galilee. "The least of all seeds" was proverbial (compare Matt 17:20).

Hearers knew the image of a great tree sheltering birds as a picture of a kingdom: the cedar God plants on Israel's mountain (Ezek 17:22-24) and Nebuchadnezzar's tree (Dan 4:10-12). Jesus surprisingly uses a garden plant, not a cedar. Mishnaic law later discouraged sowing mustard in a garden plot because it spreads (Mishnah Kilayim 3:2), which shows how invasive it was.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/mustard-seed
blocks.body: The parable is built on contrast: smallest seed / greatest plant. Mark's version doubles the contrast by repeating "when it is sown" (Mark 4:31-32). The final line, birds nesting in its shade, quotes the prophetic tree imagery and points to the nations finding shelter.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/mustard-seed
blocks.body: Loraine Boettner used the mustard seed and the leaven as key texts for postmillennialism: the kingdom begins small and grows gradually until it fills the world, through the ordinary preaching of the gospel.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/mustard-seed
blocks.body: Kenneth Gentry reads the kingdom parables of Matthew 13, including the mustard seed, as teaching the kingdom's gradual, extensive growth in history, which he sees as support for postmillennial optimism.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/mustard-seed
blocks.body:
The kingdom began with a peasant from Nazareth, twelve disciples and a cross: the smallest of seeds. It is growing into a shelter for every nation.

The Father's family is wide. The birds of the air (often an image for the Gentiles) come and rest in its branches.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/leaven
blocks.body:
Leaven was a lump of old fermented dough kept back from the last batch. Three measures (*sata*) is about forty litres of flour, enough bread for well over a hundred people: a feast. Sarah used the same quantity when she baked for the three visitors at Mamre (Gen 18:6).

Leaven is often a symbol of corruption (Exod 12:15; 1 Cor 5:6-8; Mark 8:15). Jesus here uses it positively, for the kingdom's hidden, pervasive power.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/leaven
blocks.body: Like the mustard seed, the parable turns on contrast: a small, hidden thing and a total result ("till the whole was leavened"). The verb is striking: she "hid" (*enekrypsen*) the leaven, connecting with the kingdom's hiddenness (Matt 11:25; 13:35, 44).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/leaven
blocks.body: Boettner read the leaven as an image of the gospel's gradual, permeating influence on society, until the whole world is transformed: a central image for postmillennial hope.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/leaven
blocks.body:
A woman baking for a feast pictures the Father's work. The kingdom works from within, through relationships, transforming the whole. It does not conquer by force.

"Till the whole was leavened": the parable is unashamedly hopeful about the scope of God's victory.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/hidden-treasure
blocks.body:
With frequent wars and no banks, people buried valuables in the ground (compare Matt 25:25; Josh 7:21). Owners died or fled, and treasures were forgotten. Rabbinic law discussed who owned found treasure: often it depended on whether the finder had legally acquired the land.

A labourer ploughing someone else's field would have no claim; buying the field made the treasure his.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/hidden-treasure
blocks.body: One sentence with three verbs of action (finds, hides, sells... buys) driven by one phrase: "for joy thereof". It is paired with the pearl, which follows: one man stumbles on treasure by accident, the other searches deliberately. Both end the same way: everything sold.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/hidden-treasure
blocks.body:
The man is not making a sacrifice; he is getting the bargain of his life. The kingdom is joy before it is demand.

An old line of interpretation also reads the parable the other way round: Christ is the one who gave everything to buy the field (the world) because of the treasure hidden in it, humanity. Both readings sit well with the Father's heart.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/pearl-of-great-price
blocks.body:
Pearls were among the most valuable things in the Roman world, imported from the Persian Gulf and India. Pliny the Elder calls pearls the most precious of all things. A merchant (*emporos*) was a wholesale trader who travelled.

The merchant's action is economically reckless: a dealer who sells his whole stock for a single item has nothing left to trade.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/pearl-of-great-price
blocks.body: The parable is the twin of the hidden treasure, with a variation: the merchant is actively searching ("seeking goodly pearls"). The pair shows that the kingdom may be found by accident or by quest, and the response is the same.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/pearl-of-great-price
blocks.body:
The pearl is the kingdom, and the kingdom is finally a person: Christ, in whom are "hid all the treasures of wisdom" (Col 2:3).

It also works in reverse: the Son is the merchant who found us and gave everything to make us his own. "Ye are bought with a price" (1 Cor 6:20) is the language of a lover, not a creditor.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/dragnet
blocks.body: A *sagēnē* was a large seine net, weighted below and floated above, drawn by boats or from the shore, catching everything in its path. The Sea of Galilee holds many species. Under the food laws, fish without fins and scales were unclean (Lev 11:9-12) and would be thrown away, along with fish too small or spoiled.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/dragnet
blocks.body: The parable has two scenes: the gathering at sea (indiscriminate) and the sorting on shore (discriminating). Matthew adds the explanation that repeats the conclusion of the wheat and weeds: angels separate at "the end of the age", with "furnace of fire... wailing and gnashing of teeth" (Matt 13:49-50; compare 13:42).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/dragnet
blocks.body: Most read "the end of the age" here as the final judgement at the end of history. Some partial-preterist interpreters read Matthew's harvest-and-sorting language as the judgement on the old covenant age culminating in AD 70; others in that school keep this text for the final judgement. The text itself does not settle the timing.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/dragnet
blocks.body:
The net is wide: "of every kind". The kingdom's mission is not to sort but to gather. Judgement belongs to God, not to the fishermen.

Jesus' disciples are called to be fishers of people (Mark 1:17), throwing the net widely and trusting the Father with the outcome.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/wheat-and-weeds
blocks.body:
*Zizania* is almost certainly darnel (*Lolium temulentum*), a weed that looks very like wheat until it heads, and is often infected with a toxic fungus. Its roots tangle with the wheat's. Sowing weeds in an enemy's field was a known act of revenge; Roman law addressed it.

At harvest, darnel could be separated and bundled for fuel.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/wheat-and-weeds
blocks.body: Matthew frames the parable (13:24-30) and its explanation (13:36-43) around the mustard seed and leaven. The story is mostly dialogue between servants and master: two questions ("didst not thou sow good seed?" and "wilt thou then that we go and gather them up?") and two answers ("An enemy hath done this" and "Nay... let both grow together"). The explanation identifies seven elements (sower, field, good seed, weeds, enemy, harvest, reapers) and ends with the righteous shining like the sun, echoing Daniel 12:3.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/wheat-and-weeds
blocks.body: Augustine used this parable to argue that the church in history is a mixed body, containing both true and false members, and that the kingdom of Christ is already present in the church even though the tares are not yet removed.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/wheat-and-weeds
blocks.body: "The field is the world" (Matt 13:38), not the church, although many have applied it to the church. Interpreters also differ on "the end of the age" (13:39-40): most read it as the final judgement; some partial preterists see an initial fulfilment in the judgement of AD 70. All agree the main point is patience: the servants are not to uproot.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/wheat-and-weeds
blocks.body:
The master's "Nay" forbids his servants from doing violent sorting in his name. The history of religious coercion is a history of ignoring this parable.

The Father is patient, wanting the wheat to grow. Evil is real ("an enemy hath done this"), but it does not come from the Father, and it will not have the last word.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/lost-sheep
blocks.body:
A hundred sheep was a sizable flock for a village; it might belong to an extended family. Shepherds counted the flock at night. Shepherds were often looked down on by the religiously strict because their work kept them from careful law observance.

A lost sheep lies down and will not move; the shepherd must carry it, a heavy burden, across rough country. Ezekiel 34 stands behind the story: God condemns Israel's leaders for not seeking the lost and promises to seek them himself.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/lost-sheep
blocks.body: Luke 15 is a single parable in three parts (15:3 says "this parable"): a lost sheep (one in a hundred), a lost coin (one in ten), a lost son (one in two). Each story moves through loss, search, finding, and a celebration with community, and each ends with joy in heaven. The rising stakes (1/100, 1/10, 1/2) draw the hearer toward the third story.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/lost-sheep
blocks.title: Kenneth Bailey
blocks.body: Kenneth Bailey stresses that Jesus says to his critics "What man of you, having an hundred sheep..." (Luke 15:4), asking leaders who despised shepherds to imagine themselves as one. He also notes that the owner who loses the sheep accepts responsibility for the loss, and that carrying the sheep home and restoring it to the flock pictures the costly work of salvation.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/lost-sheep
blocks.body: Irenaeus read the lost sheep as humanity in Adam: the Lord came to seek the sheep that had perished, and that sheep was man. His recapitulation theology sees Christ going over the whole ground of human life to bring Adam home.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/lost-sheep
blocks.body:
The sheep does nothing except get lost and be carried. All the action belongs to the shepherd, who is God himself coming to seek the lost (Ezek 34:11), now in the person of Jesus.

The story ends not with the sheep's repentance speech but with the shepherd's joy. The Father's heart is happiest when what he loves is home.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/lost-coin
blocks.body:
A drachma was a Greek silver coin worth about a day's wage for a labourer. Ten drachmas could be a poor woman's savings. Village houses had small windows and earth or stone floors covered with straw; a dropped coin could vanish in the cracks. Lighting a lamp in daytime used precious oil.

Some have suggested the coins were part of a bride's headdress, but there is no firm evidence for this in first-century Palestine.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/lost-coin
blocks.body: The coin story repeats the pattern of the lost sheep exactly: loss, careful search ("until she find it"), finding, a gathering of friends and neighbours (now feminine in Greek), and joy "in the presence of the angels of God". The repetition with a female character pairs a man's work (shepherding) with a woman's (housekeeping).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/lost-coin
blocks.title: Kenneth Bailey
blocks.body: Kenneth Bailey notes that Luke often pairs a story about a man with a story about a woman, and that Jesus here dares to present God through the figure of a woman searching her house, speaking to male religious leaders who might have despised both shepherds and women's work.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/lost-coin
blocks.body:
God is pictured as a woman on her knees with a lamp, sweeping. The Father's love is not limited to "masculine" images; it is patient, domestic, thorough.

The coin cannot repent or even know it is lost. Its value lies in belonging to her. Joy "in the presence of the angels" is the joy of God himself over one recovered.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/lost-son
blocks.body:
Inheritance was normally divided at the father's death (the elder son received a double portion, Deut 21:17). Asking for it while the father lived was a grave insult to his honour; the family land was the family's life. The son "gathered all together" (Luke 15:13), probably meaning he sold his share, alienating land from the family.

Feeding pigs for a Gentile was the bottom of degradation for a Jew (Lev 11:7). The "best robe", ring and shoes mark restored sonship, authority and freedom (slaves went barefoot). The fatted calf fed a whole village: the celebration was public. A dignified patriarch did not run; to do so he would hitch up his robes, a shaming act.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/lost-son
blocks.body:
The story has two acts. In the first, the younger son moves away and back: request, departure, waste, famine, "came to himself", return, welcome. His speech is prepared (15:18-19) but not finished; the father interrupts before "make me as one of thy hired servants" (15:21).

The second act mirrors the first: the elder son is also "in the field", outside; the father again goes out (15:28) to a son who insults him. The refrain "was dead, and is alive again; was lost, and is found" ends both acts (15:24, 32). The story stops without telling us whether the elder son went in, leaving the decision with the listening Pharisees.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/lost-son
blocks.title: Kenneth Bailey
blocks.body: Kenneth Bailey argues from Middle Eastern village culture that the younger son's request amounted to wishing his father dead, that the village would have treated the returning son with hostility (he discusses a Jewish ceremony of cutting off one who lost family land among Gentiles), and that the father runs and publicly humiliates himself to reach the son first and shield him. The father's costly, self-emptying love, offered to both sons, is for Bailey a picture of the cross.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/lost-son
blocks.title: Kenneth Bailey
blocks.body: Bailey also treats the elder son as equally estranged: his refusal to enter the banquet is a public insult to his father before the guests, and the father answers it not with punishment but with a second humiliating act of going out to plead with him.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/lost-son
blocks.body: N. T. Wright reads the story against Israel's story of exile and restoration: the younger son's journey into a far country and return mirrors Israel's exile and the long-awaited return, which Jesus was enacting by welcoming sinners; the grumbling elder brother corresponds to those who resented that restoration.

citations.ref: Jesus and the Victory of God (on Luke 15)

blocks.subject: entry:parable/lost-son
blocks.body:
This parable may be the clearest picture of the Father in the Gospels. He lets his son go, watches the road, runs, embraces and kisses him before any confession, and restores him fully as a son. No payment is required; the cost is borne by the father in shame and love.

And he goes out to the resentful, rule-keeping son with the same tenderness: "Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine" (Luke 15:31). Both sons misunderstood their father as a master. The gospel is that we are sons and daughters, not hired servants.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/good-samaritan
blocks.body:
The road from Jerusalem to Jericho drops about a thousand metres over some twenty-seven kilometres of desert; it was notorious for robbers. Priests and Levites served in Jerusalem in rotation and many lived in Jericho.

A man "half dead" might be dead; touching a corpse would defile a priest (Lev 21:1-3), and failing to know whether he was a fellow Jew complicated duty. Samaritans and Jews had centuries of hostility, including violent incidents in Jesus' time. Oil and wine were standard first aid, and also offerings used in Temple worship. A denarius was a day's wage; two denarii covered several days at an inn.

2 Chronicles 28:15 records Samaritans clothing, anointing and carrying wounded Judeans to Jericho, a story that may lie in the background.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/good-samaritan
blocks.body:
The passage is a debate in two rounds. Each round has a question from the lawyer, a counter-question from Jesus, an answer from the lawyer, and a command from Jesus ("this do, and thou shalt live", 10:28; "Go, and do thou likewise", 10:37). The parable sits inside the second round.

The story itself moves down and back up: robbers take, strip and leave; the priest and Levite see and pass by; the Samaritan sees, comes, binds, pours, sets, brings and pays, reversing everything the robbers did.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/good-samaritan
blocks.title: Kenneth Bailey
blocks.body: Kenneth Bailey sets out the two-round structure of the dialogue and the parable's ordered scenes. He argues that the priest was probably riding and could have carried the man, that the Samaritan's care deliberately supplies what the priest and Levite failed to give, and that by taking the man into a Jewish inn and paying for him the Samaritan exposed himself to danger and possible revenge.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/good-samaritan
blocks.title: Kenneth Bailey
blocks.body: Bailey also presents the Samaritan's costly, risky compassion as a picture of the saving love of God, who comes to rescue us at great cost to himself.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/good-samaritan
blocks.body:
The lawyer wanted to limit love. Jesus answers with a story in which the despised outsider embodies the Father's compassion (*splanchnizomai*, the same word used of the father in Luke 15:20).

Christ is the one who came down the road to where we lay, at cost to himself. Having been loved like that, we are sent to "go and do likewise", to anyone at all.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/rich-fool
blocks.body:
Inheritance disputes were often taken to rabbis. Jesus refuses the role of judge and addresses the greed behind the request (Luke 12:14-15).

In a village economy, a bumper harvest was a gift from God and an opportunity to help neighbours and the poor (Deut 15:7-11). Hoarding grain to sell high in a scarce year was considered a sin (compare Prov 11:26). "Fool" (*aphrōn*) echoes Psalm 14:1: the fool who lives as if there were no God.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/rich-fool
blocks.body: The parable is mostly the rich man's inner monologue: "What shall I do?... This will I do... I will say to my soul". He uses "I" and "my" repeatedly. God's voice breaks in at the end and answers the monologue with one question: "whose shall those things be?" (12:20). The conclusion (12:21) contrasts treasure for oneself with being "rich toward God".

blocks.subject: entry:parable/rich-fool
blocks.title: Kenneth Bailey
blocks.body: Kenneth Bailey points out that in a Middle Eastern village, major decisions were talked over with family and friends, yet this man consults no one but himself. His isolation is part of his foolishness: he has wealth but no community, and in the end no one to address but his own soul.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/rich-fool
blocks.body:
The fool is not condemned for being productive but for being alone: his abundance never becomes communion with God or neighbour.

We were made for relationship. To be "rich toward God" is to live as a child of a generous Father, sharing what we receive. The following verses (Luke 12:22-32) show the alternative: "it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom".

blocks.subject: entry:parable/great-banquet
blocks.body:
Banquets in the villages involved two invitations: the first announced the feast and let the host know how many would come (so he could decide what animal to slaughter); the second, at the hour, said "Come; for all things are now ready" (Luke 14:17). Refusing at the second stage, after accepting, was a grave public insult.

Isaiah 25:6 promises a feast of rich food for all peoples on God's mountain: the messianic banquet. The guest's pious remark (14:15) assumes the right people will be there.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/great-banquet
blocks.body: The parable follows the sequence invitation, refusal, anger, new invitation (twice), with a final verdict. The three excuses rise in rudeness: a field just bought, five yoke of oxen to test, a new wife. The servant goes out twice: first into the town's streets and lanes (the excluded within Israel), then to the highways and hedges (outsiders beyond, often read as Gentiles).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/great-banquet
blocks.title: Kenneth Bailey
blocks.body: Kenneth Bailey argues that the excuses are transparently false and insulting: no one in the Middle East buys a field without inspecting it many times, nor buys oxen without testing them first. The guests are publicly humiliating the host. The host turns his anger into grace for outsiders, and "compel them to come in" reflects the custom that an unworthy guest would politely refuse until urged, even taken by the arm.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/great-banquet
blocks.body:
The Father's table will be full. Rejection does not shrink his generosity; it widens it.

The banquet is the kingdom as shared life. The ones who come are those who know they have no claim: the poor, the disabled, the strangers. The Son spent his ministry eating with exactly these people as a sign of the feast to come.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/unjust-steward
blocks.body:
Wealthy landowners employed a steward (*oikonomos*) to run their estates and deal with tenants. Debts in olive oil and wheat suggest tenants paying rent in kind or merchants with promissory notes. A hundred measures (*batoi*) of oil and a hundred measures (*koroi*) of wheat were large amounts.

The Torah forbade charging interest to fellow Israelites (Deut 23:19), but contracts sometimes hid interest in the amounts owed; some interpreters think the steward removed his own commission or concealed interest. Others think he simply cut the master's dues.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/unjust-steward
blocks.body: The story has three scenes: the master dismisses the steward (16:1-2); the steward deliberates and acts (16:3-7), with a soliloquy ("What shall I do?") like the rich fool and the prodigal; the master praises him (16:8a). Jesus then adds a series of sayings (16:8b-13) about money, faithfulness and two masters.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/unjust-steward
blocks.title: Kenneth Bailey
blocks.body: Kenneth Bailey argues that the master was unusually merciful in dismissing rather than jailing the steward. The steward then gambles on that mercy: by reducing the debts before news of his dismissal spreads, he makes the master appear generous in the village, and the master could not reverse it without losing honour. The master praises his wisdom in staking everything on the master's generosity.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/unjust-steward
blocks.body:
If Bailey's reading is right, the parable is about trusting the master's character. The steward knows his master is merciful and throws himself entirely on that mercy.

That is exactly what the Father invites. We have nothing to bargain with, but the Father's generosity is the one thing we can stake everything on.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/rich-man-and-lazarus
blocks.body:
Purple and fine linen were the clothes of royalty and the very rich. "Fared sumptuously every day" means daily feasting, while most villagers ate meat only at festivals. Bread was used as a napkin to wipe hands at meals and then thrown away; Lazarus longs for such scraps. Dogs were unclean scavengers.

Stories of reversal after death circulated in Egyptian and Jewish folklore. Jesus uses a familiar story-form; the popular picture of Abraham's bosom and Hades as a waiting place reflects Second Temple Jewish ideas.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/rich-man-and-lazarus
blocks.body: Two halves: life (16:19-22) and after death (16:23-31). The first half contrasts gate and table, purple and sores, fullness and hunger. The second half reverses the positions and is all dialogue: three requests from the rich man (cooling water, a warning to his brothers, a messenger from the dead) and three refusals from Abraham. Lazarus never speaks. He is the only invented character in Jesus' parables given a name: *Eleazar*, "God helps".

blocks.subject: entry:parable/rich-man-and-lazarus
blocks.body: Many read this parable as a literal map of the afterlife. Others note that it uses a known folk story to make a point about wealth and repentance, so details (conversations across the gulf, a drop of water) should not be pressed as doctrine about the intermediate state. The final line, "though one rose from the dead", points forward to Jesus' own resurrection and the refusal of many to believe.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/rich-man-and-lazarus
blocks.body:
The rich man's sin is not that he was rich but that he never saw Lazarus as a brother, though he knew his name. The gulf after death had been dug by his life.

God's name for the poor man is "God helps". The Father notices those whom the comfortable ignore, and the risen Son is the one who has crossed every gulf to reach us.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/persistent-widow
blocks.body:
Widows were the symbol of vulnerability in Israel; the Torah repeatedly commands justice for them, and God calls himself their defender (Exod 22:22-24; Deut 10:18; Ps 68:5). A widow had no male relative to argue her case; in a male courtroom she should not even have been there.

Judges were expected to fear God and to care about public honour. This judge cares for neither: he cannot be shamed.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/persistent-widow
blocks.body: The story is framed by its purpose ("men ought always to pray, and not to faint", 18:1) and Jesus' closing question ("when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth?", 18:8). In the middle, the judge's soliloquy repeats the narrator's description ("though I fear not God, nor regard man"). The application is an argument from the lesser to the greater: if even this judge acts, how much more God.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/persistent-widow
blocks.title: Kenneth Bailey
blocks.body: Kenneth Bailey observes that a judge who neither fears God nor respects people has no sense of shame, so no appeal to honour will move him. The widow's only weapon is persistence. He also notes that the judge's "lest she weary me" uses a boxing word, literally "lest she give me a black eye", a comic touch.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/persistent-widow
blocks.body:
The parable is a contrast, not a comparison. God is not a reluctant judge to be worn down. He is the Father of widows who will "avenge them speedily" (Luke 18:8).

Persistent prayer is not nagging an unwilling God; it is trust that keeps standing at the Father's door, knowing he cares about justice more than we do.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/pharisee-and-tax-collector
blocks.body:
Pharisees were respected lay teachers devoted to holiness in daily life. Fasting twice a week and tithing everything exceeded the Torah's requirements. Tax collectors worked for Herod or Rome, often extorted, and were regarded as traitors and unclean.

The two men "went up into the temple to pray". Public prayer was joined to the morning and afternoon sacrifices (the *tamid*), when incense was offered and the people prayed (compare Luke 1:10). The tax collector's prayer uses the verb *hilaskomai*: "be propitious, make atonement for me".

blocks.subject: entry:parable/pharisee-and-tax-collector
blocks.body: The story is built in parallel: two men go up; each stands and prays; one prays about himself throughout (every main verb in the Pharisee's prayer is first person), the other briefly about God's mercy. The ending reverses expectation, and a closing proverb states the principle: "every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted" (18:14).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/pharisee-and-tax-collector
blocks.title: Kenneth Bailey
blocks.body: Kenneth Bailey argues that the setting is the atonement sacrifice in the Temple, so the tax collector's cry is a plea that the atonement being offered would apply to him. He also suggests the Pharisee stood apart to avoid contact with ordinary worshippers whom he considered unclean.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/pharisee-and-tax-collector
blocks.body:
"Justified" here is relational: the tax collector goes home in right relationship with God, received and set right, while the man who trusted his own record does not.

The Father is not impressed by performance and not repelled by honest need. "God be merciful to me" is the doorway into communion that is always open.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/labourers-in-the-vineyard
blocks.body:
Day labourers gathered in the market place each morning hoping to be hired. They were often landless peasants who had lost family land through debt. A denarius was the usual daily wage, roughly enough to feed a family for a day. The Torah required paying a worker's wages before sunset (Lev 19:13; Deut 24:15).

Men still standing idle at five o'clock were likely the least employable: older, weaker, or disabled. One hour's pay would not feed their families.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/labourers-in-the-vineyard
blocks.body: The parable is framed by the saying "the first shall be last, and the last first" (Matt 19:30; 20:16), which forms an inclusio. Within it, the hiring happens in five stages, and the payment reverses the order ("beginning from the last unto the first", 20:8), so the first see what the last receive. The dialogue at the end is the point: the owner's "Friend, I do thee no wrong" and his question about the "evil eye" (envy) versus his goodness.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/labourers-in-the-vineyard
blocks.body: Irenaeus read the different hours of hiring as God calling people in different ages of history, from the beginning to the end, all serving the one Lord and receiving the one reward.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/labourers-in-the-vineyard
blocks.body:
The landowner pays according to need and generosity, not merit. That offends a wage-based sense of justice, but it is restorative justice: everyone goes home able to feed their family.

Grace is the Father's justice. Those who have worked longest are invited not to resentment but to share the owner's joy in his goodness.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/two-sons
blocks.body: A son's public refusal of his father ("I will not") was shameful in a culture of honour; a polite "I go, sir" followed by disobedience was outwardly respectful but empty. The setting is the Temple courts after Jesus' entry into Jerusalem and the cleansing of the Temple. The leaders had refused to say whether John's baptism was from God (Matt 21:25-27).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/two-sons
blocks.body: This is the first of three parables of judgement addressed to the Temple leaders (two sons, wicked tenants, wedding feast, Matt 21:28-22:14). Jesus asks "What think ye?" and makes the hearers judge the story (21:31), then applies it directly to them: John came "in the way of righteousness" and tax collectors and harlots believed him; the leaders did not even "repent afterward" (*metamelomai*).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/two-sons
blocks.body:
The Father wants sons, not polite servants. The son who said no and then turned around is the one who did his will. Repentance is changing your mind and going.

The door is still open for the leaders too: the father asked both sons. The problem is not past refusal but refusing to turn.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/wicked-tenants
blocks.body:
Absentee landlords leasing estates to tenant farmers were common in Galilee, and tensions over rent paid in produce sometimes became violent. A new vineyard yielded little for the first four or five years (Lev 19:23-25).

Hearers would immediately recognise Isaiah 5:1-7, the Song of the Vineyard: God planted Israel as his vineyard, with hedge, winepress and tower, and looked for justice but found bloodshed. Jesus uses the same details (Mark 12:1).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/wicked-tenants
blocks.body: The parable is a sequence of escalating sendings: servant after servant, each treated worse, and finally "one son, his wellbeloved" (Mark 12:6). The climax is the tenants' plan ("This is the heir; come, let us kill him"), then the owner's response. A scriptural quotation (Ps 118:22-23) follows, shifting the image from vineyard to building: the stone the builders rejected becomes the head of the corner. There is a Hebrew wordplay between *ben* (son) and *ʾeven* (stone).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/wicked-tenants
blocks.body: N. T. Wright reads the parable as Jesus' retelling of Israel's story, aimed at the Temple authorities: the prophets were the rejected servants, Jesus the final messenger and son, and the coming judgement on the tenants is the destruction of the Temple and its leadership.

citations.ref: Jesus and the Victory of God (on the parable of the tenants)

blocks.subject: entry:parable/wicked-tenants
blocks.body: "The kingdom of God shall be taken from you" (Matt 21:43) has often been read as God rejecting the Jewish people. The text names the target: the chief priests and Pharisees "perceived that he spake of them" (21:45). The judgement falls on the corrupt leadership of the vineyard, not on Israel as such. Partial-preterist readers see its fulfilment in AD 70, when the Temple establishment ended. The vineyard itself passes to those who bear fruit, which includes Jewish disciples.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/wicked-tenants
blocks.body:
The owner's patience is astonishing: servant after servant, and then "they will reverence my son". This is the Father's heart, risking his beloved Son on the world's violence.

The tenants kill the son, but the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone. Resurrection turns the rejection inside out and builds a new house for all peoples.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/wedding-feast
blocks.body:
A royal wedding feast could last a week and was the social event of a generation. Refusing a king's invitation was an act of political defiance as well as personal insult.

Some have suggested hosts provided garments for guests; there is no clear evidence of this custom, but "wedding garment" would at least mean clean, festive clothing, honouring the host. Isaiah pictures salvation as being clothed with "garments of salvation... as a bridegroom" (Isa 61:10).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/wedding-feast
blocks.body: The parable has two halves: the invited guests (22:2-7) and the hall filled (22:8-14). It parallels Luke's great banquet but is heightened: the host is a king, the occasion his son's wedding, the guests violent, and the response military ("he sent forth his armies, and destroyed those murderers, and burned up their city", 22:7). The coda about the wedding garment (22:11-13) adds a second judgement scene, and the closing saying (22:14) sums it up.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/wedding-feast
blocks.body: Matthew 22:7, the king burning the city, is widely read (by critical scholars and by partial preterists alike) as pointing to the burning of Jerusalem in AD 70. Critical scholars often take this as evidence that Matthew wrote after AD 70; those who date Matthew earlier read it as Jesus' prophecy, in line with his other warnings (Luke 19:41-44). The garment has been read as righteousness, faith, repentance or love; the text does not specify.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/wedding-feast
blocks.body:
The feast is the Father's celebration of his Son's union with his bride, the people he loves. The invitation goes out to everyone, "both bad and good".

To come to a wedding is to come ready to celebrate the son. The man without a garment came on his own terms, ignoring the host. The Father welcomes all, and the welcome is meant to change us: "put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom 13:14).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/ten-virgins
blocks.body:
Weddings involved the bridegroom going, often in the evening, to fetch the bride from her father's house and bring her in procession to his own home for the feast. Young women of the village would join the procession with torches or oil lamps. Delays for negotiation over gifts were common. Lamps (*lampades*) here may be torches of rags soaked in oil, needing frequent refuelling.

Once the guests were inside, the door was shut for the night.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/ten-virgins
blocks.body: The parable divides the ten into two groups of five, wise and foolish, and repeats the contrast at each stage: preparation (oil or no oil), sleeping (all sleep), the cry at midnight, the request ("give us of your oil"), the arrival and the shut door. The closing command ties it to the Olivet theme: "Watch therefore" (25:13).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/ten-virgins
blocks.body: Most read the bridegroom's coming as Christ's final return. Partial-preterist readers note that the parable follows directly from Matthew 24, with its "this generation" time frame, and read it at least first as a warning to be ready for the crisis of AD 70, while also applying it to every generation. Readers disagree about which reading is primary.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/ten-virgins
blocks.body:
All ten fall asleep; the wise are not more anxious, just prepared. Readiness is ongoing relationship, not frantic vigilance.

"I know you not" (25:12) is the language of relationship. The Son longs to know and be known by his friends. The oil that cannot be borrowed may be the personal intimacy no one else can have for us.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/talents
blocks.body:
A talent was a unit of weight for silver, worth about six thousand denarii: roughly twenty years of a labourer's wages. Even one talent was a fortune. (The English sense of "talent" as ability comes from this parable.)

Rabbinic law treated burying entrusted money as the safest form of custody: a person who buried a deposit was not liable if it was lost. The third servant was cautious by the standards of his day, but the master expected trading.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/talents
blocks.body: The master's departure and return frame three accounts. The first two are almost word-for-word identical, with the same praise: "Well done, thou good and faithful servant... enter thou into the joy of thy lord" (25:21, 23). The third is long and different: the servant explains himself by describing the master ("I knew thee that thou art an hard man") and his fear.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/talents
blocks.body:
The third servant's problem is his picture of the master. He believes him hard and grasping, and that belief produces fear, and fear produces paralysis. He gets the master he imagined.

The first two simply enter "the joy of thy lord". The Father is generous, entrusting his children with real responsibility and inviting them into his own joy. Knowing him rightly is the key to fruitfulness.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/minas
blocks.body: A mina was worth about a hundred denarii, a few months' wages. Hearers in Jericho knew a story like this. After Herod the Great died in 4 BC, his son Archelaus travelled to Rome to have his kingship confirmed by Augustus; a Jewish delegation of fifty went to Rome to oppose him. Archelaus received only part of the kingdom and later ruled brutally. His palace was at Jericho.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/minas
blocks.body: Luke weaves two stories: the servants and their minas (19:13, 15-26) and the citizens who reject the king (19:12, 14, 27). The servants' accounts follow the pattern of Matthew's talents but with ten servants and equal amounts; only three are described. The story's frame (19:11) corrects the expectation that the kingdom would appear immediately at Jerusalem.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/minas
blocks.body: Many read the nobleman as Christ, gone to heaven to receive his kingdom and returning at the Second Coming. Others note how unlike Jesus the nobleman is (harsh, "reaping where he did not sow", ordering enemies slain before him) and read the story as Jesus subverting expectations, contrasting worldly kings like Archelaus with his own kingship revealed in Jerusalem days later. A partial-preterist reading sees the judgement of the rebellious citizens in AD 70. Each view has serious advocates.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/minas
blocks.body:
Immediately after this parable Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a colt and weeps over the city (Luke 19:28-44). Whatever the nobleman represents, the true King receives his kingdom by way of the cross, not by Roman patronage, and weeps over those who reject him.

Faithfulness with what we are given is the response of servants who trust the King's goodness.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/sheep-and-goats
blocks.body:
Palestinian shepherds ran mixed flocks of sheep and goats by day and often separated them at night, since goats need more warmth. The right hand was the place of honour.

Ezekiel 34:17 has God judging "between cattle and cattle, between the rams and the he goats". Isaiah 58:6-10 defines true fasting as feeding the hungry, sheltering the poor and clothing the naked.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/sheep-and-goats
blocks.body: Strictly this is a judgement scene with a parable image (the shepherd), not a narrative parable. It is built in two balanced halves: the King speaks to those on the right, they ask "when saw we thee...?", he answers; then the same to those on the left. The six acts of mercy (hungry, thirsty, stranger, naked, sick, prisoner) are listed four times.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/sheep-and-goats
blocks.body: Two debates: who are "the least of these my brethren" (the needy in general, or Christ's disciples and messengers), and what is the "everlasting punishment" (*kolasis aiōnios*, 25:46). *Kolasis* originally meant pruning or corrective punishment, and *aiōnios* means "of the age"; some read this as punishment belonging to the age to come rather than endless duration. The traditional view reads it as everlasting. A partial-preterist reading places the "coming" of 25:31 within the AD 70 frame of Matthew 24; most interpreters read it as the final judgement.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/sheep-and-goats
blocks.body:
The King is hidden in the least. The judgement is about whether the nations have loved as the Father loves, not whether they had the right religious vocabulary: neither group knew they were serving Christ.

This is a picture of the Son's union with humanity. He has joined himself to the hungry and imprisoned so closely that what is done to them is done to him.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/unforgiving-servant
blocks.body:
Ten thousand (*myrioi*, the largest Greek number) talents was a deliberately absurd sum: about sixty million denarii, far more than the annual tax revenue of all Herod's territories. A hundred denarii was about a hundred days' wages, a real but payable debt.

Selling a debtor with his family into slavery and debtor's prison were known practices in the Roman world, though Jewish law limited debt slavery (Lev 25:39-43).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/unforgiving-servant
blocks.body: The parable has three scenes with parallel wording. In scene one the servant falls down and begs, "Have patience with me, and I will pay thee all", and the lord, "moved with compassion", releases him (18:26-27). In scene two the fellow servant uses exactly the same words, but this time there is no compassion (18:29-30). In scene three the fellow servants report, and the lord asks, "shouldest not thou also have had compassion... even as I had pity on thee?" (18:33).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/unforgiving-servant
blocks.body:
The king's forgiveness is pure gift: the debt was unpayable. The servant took the release but never let it change his heart; he went out still living by the logic of debt.

Forgiveness is meant to be shared. The final verse (18:35) is a warning, not because the Father's love is conditional, but because refusing to forgive locks us back into the prison of debt we were released from.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/two-debtors
blocks.body:
Formal meals were semi-public; villagers could enter and watch from the edges. Guests reclined on couches with their feet pointing away from the table, which is how the woman could reach his feet.

A host normally greeted an honoured guest with a kiss, provided water for dusty feet, and might anoint the head with oil. Simon did none of these (Luke 7:44-46). A woman letting down her hair in public was considered immodest. Five hundred denarii was well over a year's wages; fifty, under two months.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/two-debtors
blocks.body: A short parable (7:41-42) sits inside a narrative. Jesus' explanation is built in three pairs, contrasting Simon's omissions with the woman's actions: no water / tears; no kiss / ceaseless kissing of the feet; no oil for the head / ointment for the feet (7:44-46). The scene ends with Jesus' declaration to the woman: "Thy sins are forgiven... Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace" (7:48, 50).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/two-debtors
blocks.title: Kenneth Bailey
blocks.body: Kenneth Bailey argues that Simon's failure to offer the customary welcome (water, kiss, oil) was a deliberate public insult to Jesus, and that the woman, already forgiven, steps in to supply the hospitality Simon withheld, at great social cost to herself.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/two-debtors
blocks.body:
The woman's love is the result of forgiveness, not its price: "her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much" means her love shows how much she has been forgiven (7:47; compare the parable's logic in 7:42).

Jesus receives the touch of a "sinner" in public, honours her above his host, and sends her away in peace. That is how the Father receives us.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/friend-at-midnight
blocks.body:
Hospitality to travellers was a sacred duty, and a guest was a guest of the whole village. Women baked bread for several days, so neighbours knew who had baked recently. A peasant family slept together on a raised platform in a single room; getting up and unbolting the door would wake the household.

*Anaideia* (KJV "importunity") means literally "lack of shame", shamelessness. Whose shamelessness is meant is debated.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/friend-at-midnight
blocks.body: Jesus' opening "Which of you shall have a friend..." (11:5) is a long question that expects the answer "No one" would refuse such a request. The story turns on a reluctant reply ("Trouble me not") and the reason for the neighbour's action (11:8). It is followed by sayings about asking, seeking and knocking, and the argument from lesser to greater: "If ye then, being evil... how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit" (11:13).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/friend-at-midnight
blocks.title: Kenneth Bailey
blocks.body: Kenneth Bailey argues that *anaideia* here should be understood as the sleeper's desire to avoid shame: if he refused, the whole village would hear that he had failed in hospitality. He gets up because of his own honour, not because the asker nags. The point is God's faithfulness to his name, not that we must badger God.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/friend-at-midnight
blocks.body:
Read with Bailey, the parable is about the character of the one we ask. Even a sleepy neighbour will rise to protect his good name. How much more will the Father, whose name we have just prayed to be hallowed (Luke 11:2), give good gifts.

The best gift is not bread but the Holy Spirit (11:13): the Father's own life shared.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/barren-fig-tree
blocks.body:
Fig trees were often planted in vineyards. A young tree might take a few years to fruit; three years of fruit-seeking after that was a fair test, and under Leviticus 19:23 fruit was not eaten for the first three years anyway. A barren tree drained the soil ("why cumbereth it the ground?").

The fig tree was a prophetic image for Israel (Hos 9:10; Mic 7:1; Jer 8:13). Digging around and manuring a tree was unusual care.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/barren-fig-tree
blocks.body: The parable is a dialogue in two speeches: the owner's verdict ("cut it down") and the vinedresser's plea ("let it alone this year also"). It ends unresolved: "if it bear fruit, well: and if not, then after that thou shalt cut it down". Like the elder brother story, the outcome is left to the hearers. It follows two warnings that end with the same refrain, "except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish" (13:3, 5).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/barren-fig-tree
blocks.body: On a partial-preterist reading, the year of grace is the time given to Jesus' generation before the judgement of AD 70, and the warnings "ye shall all likewise perish" refer to death by Roman swords and falling buildings, which happened in the war. Others read the parable more generally of God's patience before final judgement. The two readings can be held together.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/barren-fig-tree
blocks.body:
The vinedresser who pleads for more time and gets his hands dirty to give the tree life is a picture of Christ. Mercy asks for time, and mercy works.

The Father's patience is not indifference; it is love giving space for fruit. "The longsuffering of our Lord is salvation" (2 Pet 3:15).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/new-wine-old-wineskins
blocks.body:
Pious Jews fasted on set days (the Pharisee in Luke 18:12 fasted twice a week). Fasting expressed mourning and longing for God's redemption. Weddings were times when fasting was suspended.

Wineskins were goat skins. New wine continued to ferment and expand; an old skin had already stretched and become brittle, so it would burst. Unshrunk cloth sewn on an old garment would shrink at the first washing and tear it. Luke alone adds: "no man also having drunk old wine straightway desireth new: for he saith, The old is better" (5:39).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/new-wine-old-wineskins
blocks.body: Three short images answer one question. The first (bridegroom) explains the present joy and a future fast "when the bridegroom shall be taken away" (Mark 2:20). The second and third (patch and wineskins) are a matched pair, each describing something new destroying something old when wrongly combined. In the prophets, God is Israel's bridegroom (Isa 62:5; Hos 2:19-20); Jesus quietly places himself in that role.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/new-wine-old-wineskins
blocks.body:
The bridegroom is here: the joy of the Father's kingdom has arrived in the Son. Religion built for waiting cannot simply absorb the wedding.

The new wine is the life of the kingdom, the Spirit's life, and it needs new forms: table fellowship with sinners, freedom, joy. The point is not contempt for the old (Luke's last line is gently humorous) but readiness for what the Father is doing now.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/lamp-under-a-bushel
blocks.body: A Galilean house usually had one room; a small clay oil lamp set on a stand or in a wall niche lit the whole house ("it giveth light unto all that are in the house", Matt 5:15). A *modios* was a grain measure of about nine litres, a household basket. Covering a lamp with it would put it out or hide it.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/lamp-under-a-bushel
blocks.body: The saying appears in different settings with different emphases. In Matthew it follows "Ye are the light of the world" and concerns disciples' visible good works that glorify the Father (5:16). In Mark and Luke it follows the sower and concerns the hidden kingdom becoming manifest: "there is nothing hid, which shall not be manifested" (Mark 4:22), with a warning to "take heed what ye hear".

blocks.subject: entry:parable/lamp-under-a-bushel
blocks.body:
The kingdom is hidden now like a seed, but it is not meant to stay hidden. Light exists to be shared.

The goal of the disciples' visible goodness is not their own honour but that people "glorify your Father which is in heaven" (Matt 5:16): that the world sees what the Father is like.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/house-on-the-rock
blocks.body:
In Palestine many streambeds (wadis) are dry most of the year, flat and easy to build on, but winter rainstorms can turn them into torrents in hours. A builder who dug down to bedrock (Luke 6:48, "digged deep, and laid the foundation on a rock") did hard work no one would see.

Ezekiel condemns prophets who build flimsy walls and daub them with whitewash, which a storm will bring down (Ezek 13:10-14).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/house-on-the-rock
blocks.body: Two exactly parallel scenarios: hearing and doing / hearing and not doing; rock / sand; the same storm described in the same words ("the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew"); the opposite outcomes. The final phrase "and great was the fall of it" ends the Sermon on a sobering note, followed by the crowd's astonishment at Jesus' authority (Matt 7:28-29).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/house-on-the-rock
blocks.body: Some partial-preterist and many historical readers hear in the storm and the fall of a "house" an echo of the coming fall of Jerusalem's "house" (the Temple, compare Matt 23:38), built on the sand of a different way. Most read the parable as general wisdom about every life. The text supports the general reading; the historical echo is possible but secondary.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/house-on-the-rock
blocks.body:
The rock is Jesus' words, and finally Jesus himself (1 Cor 3:11). Building on him means living his way of love, enemy-love and trust in the Father described in the Sermon.

Storms come to everyone. The difference is not avoidance of trouble but what the life rests on: the Father's care revealed in the Son.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/budding-fig-tree
blocks.body:
Most trees in Palestine are evergreen; the fig loses its leaves in winter, so new leaves in spring are a clear sign that summer is coming. In Hebrew there is a wordplay between *qayitz* (summer fruit) and *qetz* (end), used by Amos (Amos 8:1-2).

Days earlier in Mark's narrative, Jesus had cursed a leafy but fruitless fig tree as an acted parable bracketing his action in the Temple (Mark 11:12-21).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/budding-fig-tree
blocks.body: A brief image (the fig tree's leaves) is applied directly ("so likewise ye, when ye shall see all these things"), then sealed by two solemn sayings: "This generation shall not pass" and "Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away". The time statement comes right after the image, binding "these things" to the hearers' generation.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/budding-fig-tree
blocks.body: Gary DeMar argues that the fig tree lesson, together with "this generation", places the fulfilment of the signs of Matthew 24:4-34 within the lifetime of Jesus' hearers, culminating in the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/budding-fig-tree
blocks.body: A popular futurist reading takes the fig tree as the modern state of Israel (1948) and "this generation" as the generation that sees it. The parable does not identify the fig tree with Israel; Luke's version says "Behold the fig tree, and all the trees" (Luke 21:29), showing it is a general seasonal image. Partial preterists read it as the sign of AD 70; futurists as the sign of the end of history.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/budding-fig-tree
blocks.body:
Jesus' point is that his disciples could read the signs and act, as Jerusalem's Christians did when they fled before the siege. The Son was not vague about what would befall his generation, and his words did not fail.

On the far side of that judgement, summer came: the gospel went to the nations, and the kingdom keeps growing.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/faithful-and-wise-servant
blocks.body: Large households had a chief slave or steward who distributed rations to the other slaves. A slave manager could rise to considerable authority, or abuse it. "Cut him asunder" (Matt 24:51) is a harsh image of severe punishment drawn from ancient practice.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/faithful-and-wise-servant
blocks.body: Two possible servants are described in parallel: the faithful one, found at work and promoted over all the master's goods; and the "evil" one, who reasons that the master is delayed, abuses fellow servants and feasts with drunkards. In Luke, the parable is followed by a principle of proportion: "unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required" (12:48).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/faithful-and-wise-servant
blocks.body:
