The test of leadership in the Father's house is feeding the household, not lording it over them. The evil servant's behaviour flows from thinking the master is absent.

Those who know the master is near, and good, serve their fellow servants. Leadership in the kingdom looks like Jesus washing feet.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/unprofitable-servants
blocks.body: A small farmer might own a single slave who did everything: ploughing, herding, and cooking. No master would invite such a slave to recline at table before himself; the social order was clear. "Unprofitable" (*achreioi*) means "owed nothing", not "worthless": they have no claim on special reward.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/unprofitable-servants
blocks.body: The parable is a sequence of three rhetorical questions expecting "No" (17:7-9), followed by an application (17:10). It works by contrast with Luke 12:37, where the returning master astonishingly "shall gird himself, and make them to sit down to meat, and will come forth and serve them".

blocks.subject: entry:parable/unprofitable-servants
blocks.body:
The parable dismantles the idea that our service puts God in our debt. We cannot earn standing with God.

But Luke has already told us what the Master is actually like: he serves his servants (Luke 12:37; 22:27). Freed from earning, we serve from love, and the Son calls us not servants but friends (John 15:15).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/tower-builder-and-warring-king
blocks.body:
A tower could be a watchtower in a vineyard (Isa 5:2) or a fortified building. Unfinished buildings drew public mockery in an honour/shame culture: "This man began to build, and was not able to finish" (14:30).

Small kingdoms facing larger ones regularly sent embassies seeking "conditions of peace" (14:32) rather than fight a war they would lose. Herod Antipas suffered a military defeat by the Nabatean king Aretas IV in AD 36.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/tower-builder-and-warring-king
blocks.body: Two parallel images ("which of you... or what king...") sit between hard sayings about discipleship: hating father and mother (a Semitic idiom for loving less), carrying one's cross (14:26-27), and forsaking all (14:33). Each image ends with a decision before action is taken.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/tower-builder-and-warring-king
blocks.body:
Following Jesus is not an impulse but a commitment that reorders every loyalty. Yet the cost is worth it, because the One we follow gives himself completely.

The second image may also hint at Israel's situation: a small nation facing Rome, better to seek "conditions of peace" than a doomed war (compare Luke 19:42). Jesus' way of peace was the wise choice.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/places-at-the-table
blocks.body:
At formal meals, couches nearest the host carried the most honour. Seating publicly displayed rank, and being moved down in front of everyone was a real humiliation. Proverbs 25:6-7 already advised: "better it is that it be said unto thee, Come up hither; than that thou shouldest be put lower".

Jesus follows with advice to the host: invite "the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind", who cannot repay (14:12-14), challenging the patronage system in which meals created obligations.

blocks.subject: entry:parable/places-at-the-table
blocks.body: Luke calls this a parable (14:7). It has two parts addressed to guests (14:8-11) and to the host (14:12-14), each with a negative command, a positive command and a reason. A proverb seals the first part: "whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased" (14:11), the same saying that ends the Pharisee and the tax collector (18:14).

blocks.subject: entry:parable/places-at-the-table
blocks.body:
Honour in the kingdom is received, not grabbed. The Son himself "took the form of a servant" and was exalted by the Father (Phil 2:7-9).

The table of the Father is not a ladder of status. Those who know they are beloved children can take the lowest seat without fear, and welcome those who cannot repay, as the Father welcomes us.
